\[ \mathbf E=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\2&1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Input IDs 0 and 2 select rows \((1,0)\) and \((2,1)\), forming an array of shape \([2,2]\). The first dimension counts positions and the second counts features per position. With tied output weights, the hidden vector \(\mathbf h=(1,0)\) takes a dot product with each embedding row:

\[ \mathbf h\mathbf E^{\mathsf T} =(1\times1+0\times0,\ 1\times0+0\times1,\ 1\times2+0\times1,\ 1\times(-1)+0\times1) =(1,0,2,-1). \]

Two features produce four candidate-token scores. Every position uses the same projection; adding the batch axis gives \([B,L,d]\to[B,L,V]\). This example shows only lookup and projection, omitting the intervening model layers.

docs.title: Walk through the tiny dimensions
docs.text: Use the tiny model widths \(V=259\), \(d=16\), and \(d_{\mathrm{ff}}=32\), with a teaching batch \(B=2\) and length \(L=4\). These illustrative dimensions do not change the actual training configuration \(B=1,L=16\). Integer inputs have shape \([2,4]\); embedding lookup produces \([2,4,16]\). The ordinary SwiGLU branch projects features to width 32 and returns them to width 16 before the residual addition. The tied head multiplies by \(E^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{16\times259}\), giving logits of shape \([2,4,259]\). A target is one integer, such as \(y=42\), selecting one of those 259 candidate scores.

docs.title: Head dimensions and the MLP intermediate width
docs.text:
The batched layout above explains how samples stack. The current model's forward handles one sequence: input \([L]\), hidden states \([L,d]\), and logits \([L,V]\). Training applies that function across samples with jax.vmap to obtain \([B,L,V]\). Do not pass the teaching table's \([B,L]\) array directly to the single-sequence interface.

For tiny's \(d=16,n_h=2,n_{\mathrm{kv}}=1\), the default head width is \(d_h=8\). Query projection produces \(2\times8=16\) values per position, reshaped to \([L,2,8]\). Key and Value each produce \(1\times8=8\) values, shaped \([L,1,8]\). Two query heads share one KV head: this is grouped-query attention (GQA). It reduces KV projection and storage, rather than halving the residual output width. The attention chapter develops the operation itself.

SwiGLU's intermediate width of 32 also does not make its final output 32-dimensional. Each row \(h\in\mathbb R^{16}\) undergoes two projections, elementwise gating, and an output projection:

\[ g=hW_g,\quad u=hW_u,\quad \operatorname{SwiGLU}(h)=(\operatorname{SiLU}(g)\odot u)W_d, \]

Here \(W_g,W_u\in\mathbb R^{16\times32}\), \(W_d\in\mathbb R^{32\times16}\), \(\odot\) denotes elementwise multiplication, and \(\operatorname{SiLU}(a)=a/(1+e^{-a})\) is applied elementwise. Both intermediate vectors have width 32; the result returns to width 16 for residual addition. This establishes the calculation and shapes. Whether this gating choice is useful is a model-design experiment.

docs.title: Minimal configuration audit
docs.text:
On the remote node, parse the resolved configuration before launching training:

.venv/bin/python -c "from ttt.config import load_experiment; import json; print(json.dumps(load_experiment('configs/book/tiny_control.json').to_dict(), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))"

The output should contain model, inner, training, and tokenizer, including resolved derived fields. If head divisibility, special-token ranges, or sequence-length limits fail, repair the configuration before waiting for XLA compilation. This command proves that the contract parses; it does not prove that the forward pass or training is correct.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• The configuration contract fixes parameter shapes, state boundaries, cost, and comparison fairness.
  • \(V\) determines the vocabulary axis of the embedding and logits; \(d\) determines residual width.
  • Resolved defaults must be written into the experiment record.
  • A tiny shape walk connects abstract fields to real tensors.
  • The next chapter computes logits, cross-entropy, and gradients from the same configuration.

docs.title: 16. Forward order: how one token travels through TTT-E2E
Do not start with a kernel
docs.text:
TTT-E2E contains several new terms: prefix, suffix, fast weights, inner loss, MLP-prime, and KV cache. The safest first reading is to follow one token through the residual stream. Once the order is clear, the implementation details have a place to attach.

The model first looks up a token ID in an embedding table. Each block then sends the hidden state through attention or a gated-delta state update, followed by an MLP. Selected later blocks have one additional fast MLP-prime. The final hidden state is normalized and projected into vocabulary logits.

token ids
   ↓
embedding
   ↓
attention / gated delta + residual
   ↓
fast MLP-prime + residual       (selected later blocks)
   ↓
static MLP or MoE + residual
   ↓
final norm → lm_head → logits

Every arrow is an interface for a shape, a mask, a cache, and a gradient. Moving MLP-prime before or after the ordinary MLP changes the algorithm. Updating it after every token, at the end of a chunk, or before the next chunk also changes the meaning of the state.

Figure 3. Two clocks in TTT. Each chunk predicts with the current fast weights and updates \( \phi \) from observed labels; \( \theta \) is updated across batches by the outer loop.

docs.title: The order implemented in this repository
docs.text:
The forward path in TTTE2EForCausalLM._block first executes the attention branch. A layer whose type is full_attention or sliding_attention calls attention. A gated_delta layer instead updates a recurrent state. The branch output is added back to the hidden state, producing the attention residual.

If the layer's parameter tree contains fast_mlp, the block reads the current fast-weight version of MLP-prime. The corresponding architecture switch is use_fast_mlp. The branch applies normalization, SwiGLU, and optional post-normalization, then adds the result to the residual stream. Only afterward does the block execute the ordinary static MLP or MoE branch.

The conceptual order is therefore:

attention / gated delta
→ fast MLP-prime
→ static MLP or MoE

This is an additional adaptation path, not a replacement of the original feed-forward network. If fast weights are absent, the configuration and parameter tree do not silently create a fast path. A shape check can confirm that tensors fit, but it cannot confirm that this semantic order is correct.

docs.title: Prefix and suffix
docs.text:
The configuration divides the block stack into a prefix and a suffix. The prefix runs the static part once and produces hidden states for every position. The suffix consumes those hidden states while carrying the updateable fast weights.

This division avoids repeating all static computation inside the inner loop, but it creates an alignment requirement. The prefix cache, hidden states, positions, and masks must describe the same sequence positions that the suffix scans. A suffix is not an independent piece of text; it receives representations produced for those exact positions.

The current sequence_loss pads inputs, runs model.prefix, then reshapes its hidden features into chunks of ttt_chunk_size. It scans the suffix chunk by chunk. The fast state starts at initial_fast_weights(params), and each complete chunk commits the state used by the next. An incomplete final chunk still scores real targets, but commits no fast-weight update at all, including updates from those real targets. This matches the streaming path's complete-chunk rule.

docs.title: Why fast weights are not ordinary parameters
docs.text:
Ordinary parameters are shared by many examples and updated by the outer optimizer. They survive from one training step to the next. Fast weights are temporary task or session state: an inner loss can change them while a sequence is being processed.

Use two time indices to keep the clocks separate:

\[ \theta_{k+1} = \operatorname{AdamW}\!\left( \theta_k,\, \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{outer}} \right), \] \[ \phi_{c+1} = \phi_c -\eta_{\mathrm{inner}} \nabla_\phi \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inner}} \left(\theta,\phi_c;X_c,Y_c,M_c\right). \]

Here \(k\) counts outer training steps and \(c\) counts complete inner-update chunks; \(X_c,Y_c,M_c\) are a chunk's inputs, targets, and mask. This equation shows plain gradient descent; the implementation also clips gradients, as the next chapter explains. Static parameters \(\theta\) include the learned MLP-prime initialization, from which initial_fast_weights(params) obtains \(\phi_0\). That initialization participates in outer training. The adapted values \(\phi_1,\phi_2,\ldots\) belong to a sequence or session and are not written back as global AdamW parameters. Learning the initialization and storing the adapted session value in the optimizer are different operations.

docs.title: Prefix prediction, label use, and causality
docs.text:
A safe causal update has this order:

use the current fast state to predict a chunk's targets
→ wait until all its labels are observed, then compute inner loss
→ commit the new fast state
→ use it for the next chunk

The label used for an inner update must be available at the point where the update happens. If a suffix label is used to update the state before the same position is predicted, the model receives future information and the measured loss is too optimistic.

The test is simple to state: change a later token and compare logits at every earlier position. Earlier logits must remain unchanged up to numerical tolerance. Earlier/later refers to time positions; prefix/suffix above refers to layers. These are different axes. This test catches semantic leakage that tensor-shape tests cannot see.

The inner step uses jax.value_and_grad with respect to fast weights, then applies sgd_update. The outer differentiation through sequence_loss can follow that update and introduce second derivatives. jax.checkpoint recomputes values to save memory; it does not automatically truncate these gradients. A first-order approximation requires an explicit choice of which derivative paths to stop. Rematerialization is not itself such an approximation.

docs.title: A small chunk calculation
docs.text:
Let the sequence length be \(8\) and the chunk size be \(4\). The numbers \(0\) through \(7\) below are code array indices; in the book's mathematical notation they correspond to positions \(1\) through \(8\):

chunk 0: positions 0, 1, 2, 3
chunk 1: positions 4, 5, 6, 7

Chunk 0 predicts with \(\phi_0\), obtains \(\mathcal{L}_0\), and updates to \(\phi_1\). Chunk 1 predicts with \(\phi_1\) and obtains \(\mathcal{L}_1\). Now consider a separate sequence with six target positions: its final chunk has two real targets and two padding positions. Real targets still contribute to loss; padding weights are zero. Because the chunk is incomplete, the current implementation retains the whole previous fast state \(\phi_1\), without committing an update from the two real targets either.

This is why chunk size is an algorithmic variable, not merely a batching detail. A smaller chunk lets the fast state observe context more often but increases scan and update overhead. It also changes the boundary through which gradients and caches are carried.

docs.title: How to validate that the forward pass is semantically correct
docs.text:
A useful validation set contains at least four checks:

  1. Check the dense model without fast MLP and C with the module present but updates disabled separately; they differ in architecture, so their logits need not agree.
  2. Change a later token and verify that every earlier logit remains unchanged.
  3. Compare full-sequence execution with prefill/decode streaming under the same initial state and masks.
  4. When changing chunk size, record whether it is an intended algorithm change or only an implementation optimization.

These are validation goals, not a claim that one script implements them all. The next section lists exactly what the GPU script executes and records; other comparisons require separate evidence.

docs.title: Shape walk for one token
docs.text:
Use the tiny configuration with \(d=16\), \(V=259\), batch \(B=1\), and \(L=4\) positions:

Stage Teaching object Batched shape Check Input input_ids \([1,4]\) every integer is in \([0,259)\) Embedding hidden \([1,4,16]\) token IDs become residual vectors Attention/delta residual \([1,4,16]\) only permitted history is read MLP-prime fast branch \([1,4,16]\) intermediate width returns to 16 Output logits \([1,4,259]\) every position has 259 candidate scores

This table describes the conceptual batched layout. The current model's forward takes single-sequence input_ids of shape \([L]\), has hidden states \([L,d]\), and returns logits \([L,V]\). Training adds the batch axis outside this function with jax.vmap; the table's \([B,L]\) array is not a direct input to the single-sequence interface.

docs.title: A numerical causality assertion
docs.text:
For a sequence with four input positions, run twice with identical initial parameters and mask, changing only input index 3 from 18 to 19. Indices 0, 1, and 2 all precede that change, so logits at all three must agree. For single-sequence logits of shape [L,V], the conceptual assertion is:

max_abs_diff(logits_a[0:3, :], logits_b[0:3, :]) <= tolerance
max_abs_diff(logits_a[3:, :], logits_b[3:, :]) may be > 0

Here max_abs_diff means the maximum elementwise absolute difference; it is explanatory notation, not a repository API. Failing the first line indicates that future information influenced an earlier prediction. Changes are allowed only from index 3 onward. Declare the tolerance with dtype and comparison method rather than widening it merely to pass.

docs.title: Minimal validation
docs.text:
On a remote GPU node, run bash scripts/validate_gpu.sh outputs/gpu-validation.json. This executes the built-in tiny cases in ttt/validate.py; it does not read the previous chapter's C/F configuration files. Each case checks finite loss and gradients, compares sequence_loss with TTTSession.observe, and asserts causality under future-token perturbation.

The successful report has top-level environment, passed, and cases. Each case records name, tokens, loss, finite_gradients, logits_max_error, compilation_seconds, training_seconds, state_bytes, and inner_updates. The logit error is the sequence/streaming difference, not a separate causality-error field. A failed report includes passed=false, exception type, message, and environment.

The script does not export full configuration, masks, initial parameters, state shapes, or restore comparisons. Case settings and seeds live in its source, so preserve the source revision. It requires an available GPU but does not check a particular model or multi-GPU count. Recovery is covered in Chapter 3. A tiny pass covers only the cases actually listed; the next chapter explains the connection between inner and outer gradients.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Forward order determines what each residual path and state can observe.
  • The fast-weight initialization participates in outer training; adapted values belong to a sequence or session.
  • Prefix/suffix, chunks, and masks must use the same position coordinate.
  • Causality requires a numerical future-token perturbation test.
  • The next chapter expands this state transition into inner and outer gradient paths.

docs.title: 17. Inner and outer loops: learning how to adapt
Two clocks behind one prediction
docs.text:
The previous chapter followed a token through the forward path. Now imagine a paragraph that introduces an unfamiliar term. The model has made a prediction and has just observed the correct next token. We want that observation to help with the rest of the paragraph, and we want many training texts to teach the model how to use such observations. These are different problems, requiring different updates.

We keep the tiny hidden width \(d=16\) and chunk length \(C=4\). By the end of this chapter you should be able to identify the fast state used by a chunk, the label that completes its update, and the outer-gradient path through that update. The prerequisites are prefix/suffix computation and token cross-entropy. We will still derive the chain rule rather than treating automatic differentiation as an explanation.

Let \(\theta_k\) denote static parameters at outer training step \(k\), and let \(\phi_c\) be fast weights at the beginning of chunk \(c\) in one sequence. Here \(c\) counts chunks, not tokens. At the start of a sequence the code extracts \(\phi_0\) from \(\theta_k\); it does not sample a fresh set of random matrices.

hold theta_k fixed
  phi_0 → chunk 0 predictions and loss → phi_1 → chunk 1 → phi_2
                    differentiate sequence loss w.r.t. theta_k
                                      ↓
                                  theta_{k+1}

The inner loop changes sequence state. The outer loop changes the static parameters and learned fast-weight initialization used by later training examples. A final \(\phi\) from one independent training sample is not used directly to initialize the next sample. At inference, retaining it means continuing the same session.

docs.title: From token cross-entropy to a fast-weight update
docs.text:
Start with an intentionally simplified two-class language model. Its vocabulary contains \(A,B\); one scalar fast parameter \(\phi\) produces logits \(\mathbf z=(0,\phi)\). There is no attention or MLP in this example. It isolates the derivative. For target \(B\),

\[ p_\phi(B)=\frac{e^\phi}{1+e^\phi},\qquad \ell(\phi)=-\log p_\phi(B)=\log(1+e^\phi)-\phi. \]

Differentiating the two terms gives

\[ \frac{d\ell}{d\phi} =\frac{e^\phi}{1+e^\phi}-1 =p_\phi(B)-1. \]

At \(\phi_0=0\), both candidates have probability \(0.5\), the loss is \(\log2\approx0.6931\), and the gradient is \(-0.5\). With learning rate \(1\), SGD gives \(\phi_1=0-1(-0.5)=0.5\). Substituting back gives \(p_{\phi_1}(B)\approx0.6225\) and loss \(0.4741\). This is a complete hand calculation of an observation changing a subsequent prediction.

If two positions have targets \(B,A\), and this toy model uses the same \((0,\phi)\) at both positions, their mean gradient at zero is \([(-0.5)+0.5]/2=0\). No update need not mean a software bug; the model may lack a representation that distinguishes the contexts. Real logits depend on position-specific hidden states, so the gradient is

\[ \nabla_\phi\mathcal L_{\mathrm{inner}} =\frac{1}{\sum_t m_t} \sum_t m_t \left(\frac{\partial\mathbf z_t}{\partial\phi}\right)^{\mathsf T} (\mathbf p_t-\operatorname{onehot}(y_t)), \qquad \sum_t m_t>0. \]

First compute each vocabulary logit's error, then propagate it through the Jacobian from fast parameters to logits. In the scalar example, the first logit has derivative \(0\) and the second has derivative \(1\), leaving \(p(B)-1\). The implementation differentiates a whole pytree of matrices; matrix entries do not directly regress onto the numerical values of token IDs.

A Jacobian is a table of derivatives: entry \(v,i\) describes how logit \(v\) changes when parameter \(i\) changes slightly. Flattening fast matrices into \(n_\phi\) parameters gives a \([V,n_\phi]\) table. Its transpose multiplies the \([V]\) error vector to produce a \([n_\phi]\) parameter gradient. Automatic differentiation usually computes this product directly without storing the entire table.

docs.title: Clipping changes the step, not the label
docs.text:
As a separate arithmetic illustration, consider \(\ell(\phi)=\tfrac12(\phi-3)^2\). At \(\phi_0=1\), the gradient is \(-2\), and SGD with learning rate \(0.5\) reaches \(2\). This squared-error example explains update arithmetic; it is not the actual inner objective.

For gradient leaves \(g_j\), the code computes the global norm and update

\[ \widetilde{\|g\|}_2=\sqrt{\sum_j\sum_i g_{j,i}^2+10^{-12}}, \quad a=\min\left(1,\frac{\kappa}{\widetilde{\|g\|}_2}\right), \quad \phi'=\phi-\eta_{\mathrm{inner}}ag. \]

The small value inside the square root matches code and avoids numerical problems in higher derivatives at zero gradient. With \(\kappa=0.5\), the scalar gradient is multiplied by approximately \(0.25\), giving approximately \(1.25\). This constrains the length of the entire gradient tree, not each entry separately or the parameter norm. Record learning rate, clipping threshold, gradient norm, and update norm separately; a small state change cannot identify its cause.

docs.title: Four input positions require five tokens
docs.text:
A block of \(C\) predictions needs \(C\) labels. Inputs \(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\) require targets \(x_2,x_3,x_4,x_5\). An online reader at \(x_4\) does not yet know the final label \(x_5\); that observation must arrive before the update completes.

Stage Mathematical input positions State used for prediction Labels needed for update Resulting state chunk 0 \(1,\ldots,4\) \(\phi_0\) \(x_2,\ldots,x_5\) \(\phi_1\) chunk 1 \(5,\ldots,8\) \(\phi_1\) \(x_6,\ldots,x_9\) \(\phi_2\) fewer than 4 remaining prediction positions remaining positions current \(\phi\) available real labels score, but retain old \(\phi\)

Training already has the entire sequence in memory but must preserve the same causal order: predict this block first, and let later blocks use its update. sequence_loss pads the tail for fixed shapes, scores valid labels, and conditionally retains old fast weights for an incomplete chunk. A nonzero tail mask alone is not permission to update.

docs.title: Mapping equations to functions and arrays
docs.text:
In ttt/inner_loop.py, inner_step runs the suffix, computes cross-entropy, differentiates fast weights, and calls sgd_update. Its output cache comes from pre-update prediction; historical KV is not re-encoded after the update. Optional track_post_loss evaluates the same block again. It is an adaptation diagnostic, not new held-out evidence.

Code object Single-sequence shape or type Meaning hidden \([C,d]\) prefix output targets \([C]\) next-token integer IDs mask \([C]\) target weights fast_weights pytree arrays changed by the inner loop cache tuple of layer states history read by the suffix scan carry \((\phi_c,\text{cache}_c)\) state passed to the next chunk

sequence_loss uses two levels of lax.scan and jax.checkpoint to recompute intermediate values during backward. This checkpoint is computational rematerialization, not a checkpoint file on disk. It reduces saved activations without itself detaching gradients.

docs.title: Combining examples in the outer objective
docs.text:
If sample \(b\) has total supervision weight \(n_b=\sum_t m_{b,t}\) and mean loss \(\mathcal L_b\), the batch's weighted mean is

\[ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{batch}} =\frac{\sum_b n_b\mathcal L_b}{\sum_b n_b}, \qquad \sum_b n_b>0. \]

For binary masks, \(n_b\) is the valid-target count. Combining 100 targets at mean loss 2 with 2 targets at mean loss 10 gives \(220/102\approx2.157\), not \((2+10)/2=6\). The code substitutes a safe denominator of 1 and returns zero NLL only when the total weight is zero. A positive fractional denominator below 1 must retain its actual value. An all-zero mask supplies no supervision; zero NLL is not evidence of useful training or an unchanged optimizer state.

ttt/training.py differentiates the objective with respect to static parameters and passes gradients to the outer Optax optimizer. MoE regularization enters the training objective while nll remains separate. The inner learning rate has its own warmup, moving linearly from inner_lr_start to its target. The outer schedule uses warmup and cosine decay. Fix and record both schedules in a comparison.

docs.title: Why the outer derivative contains second derivatives
docs.text:
Let the initialization be \(\phi_0(\theta)\). First expand one SGD update when clipping is inactive:

\[ \phi_1=\phi_0(\theta)-\eta g(\theta,\phi_0(\theta)), \qquad g=\nabla_\phi\mathcal L_{\mathrm{inner}}. \]

Set \(J_0=d\phi_0/d\theta\), and assume \(\eta\) does not depend on \(\theta\) for this step. Then

\[ \frac{d\phi_1}{d\theta} =J_0-\eta\left( \frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta} +\frac{\partial g}{\partial\phi}J_0 \right), \] \[ \frac{d\mathcal L_{\mathrm{outer}}}{d\theta} =\frac{\partial\mathcal L_{\mathrm{outer}}}{\partial\theta} +\frac{\partial\mathcal L_{\mathrm{outer}}}{\partial\phi_1} \frac{d\phi_1}{d\theta}. \]

Because \(g\) is already a first derivative, differentiating it introduces second-order terms. A full meta-gradient retains them. A common first-order approximation ignores derivatives of \(g\) while retaining \(J_0\); applying stop_gradient to all of \(\phi_1\) also removes the initialization path. These are different approximations and cannot both be described simply as “first order.” See MAML for the original background on learning an adaptable initialization.

The earlier binary model makes the three outcomes calculable by hand. Set \(\phi_0=\theta=0\), inner target \(B\), and learning rate 1, giving \(\phi_1=0.5\). Since \(g(\phi)=p_\phi(B)-1\), we have \(dg/d\phi=p_\phi(B)(1-p_\phi(B))=0.25\) at zero. Consequently, \(d\phi_1/d\theta=1-0.25=0.75\).

To isolate the future-prediction derivative, temporarily choose the next position's target \(A\) as the outer objective: \(\mathcal L_{\rm future}=\log(1+e^{\phi_1})\). Its derivative with respect to \(\phi_1\) is \(0.6225\). The full chain rule gives approximately \(0.6225\times0.75=0.4669\); ignoring the inner gradient's derivative gives \(0.6225\); detaching all of \(\phi_1\) gives \(0\). These are different computations, not three ways to write the same gradient. The real sequence objective includes losses at other positions; this isolated future term makes the path through adaptation visible.

When clipping activates, replace \(g\) with \(a(g)g\); its derivative includes the clipping scale's dependence. The unclipped derivation is therefore not the whole implementation. The current inner loop has no configurable FOMAML switch. Its outer loss differentiates through the implemented update. Adding a first-order comparison requires specifying which derivative is removed and checking that computation; an experiment report cannot claim an existing option that the code does not expose.

docs.title: Minimal remote validation and report reading
docs.text:
On a remote GPU node with dependencies installed, run from the repository root:

bash scripts/validate_gpu.sh outputs/ch17/validation.json

This runs the built-in tiny cases in ttt.validate. It does not load your formal training corpus or start a 125M run. The report has passed, environment, and cases. Actual case fields include loss, finite_gradients, logits_max_error, compilation_seconds, training_seconds, state_bytes, and inner_updates.

Success requires finite loss and gradients, streaming error within the script's \(10^{-3}\) limit, and the internal causality assertion after modifying future tokens. Causality has no separate JSON boolean: passed=true is written only after the assertion succeeds. If no GPU is found, inspect the backend first. For excessive error, inspect chunk labels and caches; for nonfinite gradients, inspect learning rate, clipping, and precision. Failure reports contain passed=false, error_type, and error.

docs.title: Summary: an update is not a quality improvement
docs.text:
We have connected token loss, fast-weight gradients, later chunk state, and the outer derivative. The functional report establishes the listed checks for small configurations. It does not establish generalization on a real corpus, cover every length, or test session snapshot recovery.

A C2/F2 (or C4/F4) comparison fixes architecture, initialization, data, budget, and outer schedules, changing only whether the inner update runs. The number names the recipe's full-attention layer count. Removing MLP-prime is a separate structural ablation. The next chapter carries the same label-availability constraint into token-by-token inference, where caches, incomplete chunks, and fast weights must advance together.

docs.title: 18. Attention, caches, and streaming inference
Why generating a sentence requires state
docs.text:
The previous chapter established when fast weights change. We now change the execution pattern from a whole sequence to tokens arriving one at a time. Suppose the model has read “The weather today” and receives another token. It needs the known prefix to continue predicting. Recomputing the prefix on every call repeats the same historical key and value calculations. A KV cache stores those intermediate results to avoid that repetition.

We retain the tiny example with hidden width \(d=16\) and TTT chunk length \(C=4\). First we calculate attention with two-dimensional vectors; then we track a session from \(x_1\) through \(x_6\). The prerequisites are matrix multiplication and softmax, whose roles we connect explicitly below. The goal is to explain which history each step reads, which state it writes, and why future tokens remain inaccessible.

Figure 4. From sequence processing to token processing. Follow the new token to its query and follow the historical arrows to the keys and values it can read. The figure explains the cache; a TTT session additionally retains fast weights, positions, and an unfinished chunk.

docs.title: From retrieving relevant information to two positions
docs.text:
Attention is a weighted retrieval operation. A query represents what the current position needs, a key represents what a candidate position offers, and a value carries the information retrieved. These are learned linear projections, not human-assigned semantic labels:

\[ Q=HW_Q,\qquad K=HW_K,\qquad V=HW_V. \]

Here \(H\in\mathbb R^{L\times d}\) contains one sequence's hidden states, \(L\) is its length, and one head has \(Q,K\in\mathbb R^{L\times d_h}\). The dot product \(q_t^\top k_s\) measures compatibility in the learned representation space. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_h}\) controls its scale: if the components are independent with zero mean and unit variance, the dot product has variance \(d_h\), and the scaled result has variance 1. This motivates the scaling; it does not assert that trained queries and keys follow those assumptions exactly.

Set \(L=d_h=2\), using already projected matrices:

\[ Q=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\quad K=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad V=\begin{bmatrix}10&0\\0&10\end{bmatrix}. \]

Before masking, the scores are

\[ S=\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt2} =\begin{bmatrix}0.7071&0\\0.7071&0\end{bmatrix}. \]

Position 1 must not read position 2 in an autoregressive language model. Otherwise, an input from the future might reveal the answer it is supposed to predict. An additive causal mask contributes zero to allowed scores and negative infinity to forbidden scores:

Query position \ historical position \(s=1\) \(s=2\) \(t=1\) \(0\): allowed \(-\infty\): future \(t=2\) \(0\): allowed \(0\): allowed

Write this additive attention mask as \(\mathcal M\), distinguishing it from the data chapters' loss mask. Applying softmax independently to each row gives weights \(A\) and output \(O\):

\[ \mathcal M=\begin{bmatrix}0&-\infty\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad A=\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}(S+\mathcal M) =\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0.6698&0.3302\end{bmatrix}, \] \[ O=AV=\begin{bmatrix}10&0\\6.698&3.302\end{bmatrix}. \]

Position 1 uses only the first value; position 2 mixes both. Keeping the diagonal is correct: the representation at input position \(t\) includes \(x_t\) and predicts \(x_{t+1}\). Observing the current input is different from observing its next-token label. This scaled dot-product construction and causal masking follow the original Transformer formulation.

docs.title: What a KV cache does and does not store
docs.text:
In ordinary causal attention, a new token needs its own \(q,k,v\); its key and value are appended to the cache. Historical keys and values remain available, and the new query compares against the currently visible keys. A KV cache is intermediate computation, not a new set of trainable parameters, and it cannot replace model weights.

For memory estimates, batched inference is often described with the conceptual layout \([B,n_{\rm kv},L,d_h]\), where \(B\) is the number of sessions and \(n_{\rm kv}\) the number of KV heads. This repository's KVCache serves a single session and actually stores keys and values as \([\text{capacity},n_{\rm kv},d_h]\), plus a positions array of length capacity. An assertion copied from the conceptual layout would incorrectly reject this implementation.

If each key/value element uses \(b\) bytes, and all layers share the same length and head configuration, the KV data alone occupy approximately

\[ M_{\rm KV}=2B\,n_{\rm layers}\,n_{\rm kv}\,L\,d_h\,b. \]

With \(B=1\), \(n_{\rm kv}=2\), \(L=4096\), \(d_h=64\), and \(b=2\), this is \(2{,}097{,}152\) bytes, or \(2\) MiB, per layer; 12 layers use \(24\) MiB. This excludes weights, fast weights, activations, workspace, positions, and allocator overhead. With grouped-query attention, several query heads share fewer KV heads; use the KV head count in the formula.

Three lengths must remain distinct: observed token count, allocated cache capacity, and the attention window currently visible. TTTSession grows capacity, while sliding attention restricts visible history through positions and masking. A window constraint does not establish that the allocator holds exactly “window length times bytes per token.” Inspect actual arrays and device memory statistics.

docs.title: Prefill and decode follow the same timeline
docs.text:
Prefill processes an already supplied prefix; decode processes a subsequently arriving token. These names describe call patterns, not different causal rules. In this repository, both prefill and decode ultimately use observe. Splitting the same token stream across calls should preserve its prediction and update semantics.

Continue with \(C=4\). The four inputs \(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4\) have targets \(x_2,x_3,x_4,x_5\). After observing \(x_4\), the last label is still unavailable. The following table assumes enabled inner updates and a nonempty fast-weight tree. The cache column describes valid history; allocated capacity can be larger.

After the call position pending_count Pending targets Fast weights updates Valid cache reset 0 0 none \(\phi_0\) 0 none prefill \(x_1,\ldots,x_4\) 4 4 \(x_2,x_3,x_4\) \(\phi_0\) 0 \(x_1,\ldots,x_4\) decode \(x_5\) 5 1 none \(\phi_1\) 1 \(x_1,\ldots,x_5\) decode \(x_6\) 6 2 \(x_6\) \(\phi_1\) 1 \(x_1,\ldots,x_6\)

When \(x_5\) arrives, the program first completes the previous chunk's labels, performs its update, and then processes \(x_5\) with \(\phi_1\) to predict \(x_6\). This does not leak \(x_5\) into the prediction of \(x_5\), which was already made while processing \(x_4\). “None” in the third row means the new chunk has no known target yet, not that the model has failed to observe \(x_5\).

Historical suffix caches may have been produced under earlier fast weights. This implementation retains them instead of re-encoding all history after every update. Therefore, rerunning the entire prefix with the latest \(\phi\) is not a valid equality reference. Compare sequence_loss and TTTSession under the same chunk boundaries and cache history rules. Their agreement establishes that the batch and streaming paths implement the same algorithm.

docs.title: A session is jointly evolving state
docs.text:
Saving KV alone cannot restore TTT inference. The following fields jointly determine the next call:

State Why it matters fast_weights Determine the current adapted computation cache, position Determine visible history, positional encoding, and writes pending_features, pending_targets, pending_count Reconstruct the unfinished inner-loop sample chunk_cache, chunk_start Retain the suffix history at the current chunk's start last_logits Preserve the most recent next-token distribution updates, rng_key Preserve update counts and the random process

ttt/session_store.py saves arrays together with metadata. Loading checks model revision, configuration, inner-loop settings, array shapes and dtypes, token ranges, positions, and chunk boundaries. The format version is 2, and loading targets the first local device. These are implementation constraints, not a promise of arbitrary model-version or distributed-topology migration.

A meaningful restoration check saves in the middle of a chunk, sends the same suffix through the original and restored sessions, and compares logits, fast weights, update counts, and positions. It should also cover a full chunk whose final target has not yet arrived. The repository contains tests/test_session_store.py and tests/test_runtime_consistency.py. The single-GPU validation script does not call the former; its success cannot stand in for session restoration coverage.

docs.title: Connecting implementation to evidence
docs.text:
Question Code location Key/value layout, RoPE, causal and window masks ttt/models/ttt_e2e/attention.py Prefill/decode, arriving labels, chunk completion ttt/runtime.py Chunk-based training reference ttt/inner_loop.py Saving sessions and checking restores ttt/session_store.py GPU causality and streaming checks ttt/validate.py

After completing environment setup, run this command at the repository root on a remote GPU machine. It does not require local-computer testing.

bash scripts/validate_gpu.sh outputs/ch18/validation.json

Success produces validation.json and a sibling environment.json; the former has top-level passed: true. Every case includes logits_max_error and inner_updates. Full-sequence and streaming logits must have maximum absolute error below \(10^{-3}\). The script also changes tokens in the second half and checks that first-half logits remain unchanged within its numerical tolerances. That check is the operational counterpart of forbidding position 1 from reading position 2.

For a streaming mismatch, first inspect token order, target offsets, and update timing. If failure occurs only across a window or capacity expansion, inspect positions, capacity, and masks. For a CUDA failure before any case starts, inspect the environment report and JAX device discovery. This command does not validate on-disk session restoration, arbitrary lengths, every attention backend, or improved language quality.

We have connected the attention equations to a session timeline. The next chapter adds another decision to the same hidden state: which subset of parameters should process this token?

docs.title: 19. MoE: letting tokens choose a computation path
More stored parameters need not mean more work per token
docs.text:
The previous chapter explained how a token reads history. We now keep attention and change the feed-forward network: prepare several sets of expert parameters and select only a few for each token. An expert is typically an MLP; the small network that selects experts is the router. Together they form a mixture of experts, or MoE.

Stored parameter count and activated parameter count are different quantities. With \(n_{\rm exp}\) SwiGLU experts of hidden width \(d\) and intermediate width \(d_{\rm ff}\), expert parameters total approximately \(3n_{\rm exp}dd_{\rm ff}\), ignoring biases. Selecting \(k_{\rm sel}\) experts makes the expert forward multiplications correspond mainly to \(3k_{\rm sel}dd_{\rm ff}\) parameters per token. Routing, sorting, communication, and memory movement still cost time; these counts are not GPU speedup factors.

We first route four tokens to one of two experts and trace sorting and restoration by hand. Then we extend the picture to top-2 routing and the repository's four-expert, two-device validation. Prerequisites are hidden states, softmax, and feed-forward matrix shapes. We initially omit shared experts, fast routing, and memory corrections, and place them in the framework at the end.

Figure 5. One MoE forward pass. Track both token identity and expert grouping: computation may reorder rows, but the residual stream needs the original order. Capacity illustrates a common design choice; the current reference path does not drop tokens according to a capacity limit.

docs.title: From routing scores to a weighted output
docs.text:
For hidden state \(h_t\in\mathbb R^d\), the router produces \(n_{\rm exp}\) logits and converts them to probabilities:

\[ r_t=W_rh_t,\qquad p_{t,e}=\frac{\exp(r_{t,e})}{\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\rm exp}}\exp(r_{t,j})}. \]

This equation uses column vectors. Code generally places tokens in matrix rows, with linear handling the corresponding transpose. The current implementation selects top-\(k_{\rm sel}\) using \(r_{t,e}+b_e\), where \(b_e\) is load_bias. Mixing weights come from the original \(p_{t,e}\), normalized within the selected set \(S_t\):

\[ S_t=\operatorname{TopK}(r_t+b,k_{\rm sel}),\qquad \widetilde p_{t,e}= \frac{p_{t,e}}{\sum_{j\in S_t}p_{t,j}},\qquad y_t=\sum_{e\in S_t}\widetilde p_{t,e}F_e(h_t). \]

\(F_e\) denotes expert \(e\). Selection scores and mixing weights are distinct: a load bias can change who is selected without being inserted into the probability softmax. Set \(b=0\) in the following example, so ranking by probability agrees with ranking by logits.

Original token index (code) \(p_{t,1}\) \(p_{t,2}\) Top-1 expert 0 0.8 0.2 \(E_1\) 1 0.4 0.6 \(E_2\) 2 0.7 0.3 \(E_1\) 3 0.3 0.7 \(E_2\)

A single selected expert receives normalized weight 1. The two experts receive tokens \([0,2]\) and \([1,3]\). Grouped row order is \([0,2,1,3]\), with group sizes \([2,2]\); output must return to \([0,1,2,3]\). Computing every expert correctly still gives the wrong model if token 2's result is handed to token 1.

With top-2, each token produces two token–expert assignments, temporarily duplicating input rows. For three expert probabilities \((0.6,0.3,0.1)\), the selected weights become \((2/3,1/3)\). If the selected expert outputs are \((2,0)\) and \((0,3)\), the combined output is \((4/3,1)\). Restore each assignment before aggregating by original token; the second path must survive grouping.

Top-1 here is a sorting example. Under this implementation's renormalization, its selected weight is always 1, and the discrete selection does not provide the ordinary derivative. The language-model loss therefore does not train the router through this mixing weight; auxiliary terms can still provide gradients. Do not generalize this teaching example to the training definition of every top-1 MoE. The two-device validation uses top-2.

docs.title: Capacity and load are different questions
docs.text:
When every token prefers the same expert, sequential processing remains logically possible, but that expert can become a computation or memory bottleneck. Fixed-capacity implementations commonly allocate

\[ C_{\rm exp}= \left\lceil\gamma\frac{T_{\rm tok}k_{\rm sel}}{n_{\rm exp}}\right\rceil \]

slots per expert, where \(\gamma\) is the capacity factor and \(T_{\rm tok}\) the token count in one routing operation. Our example has \(T_{\rm tok}=4\), \(k_{\rm sel}=1\), \(n_{\rm exp}=2\), and \(\gamma=1\), giving capacity 2. The balanced assignment fits exactly. A separate routing outcome sending all four tokens to \(E_1\) overflows by two slots; the system must define dropping, overflow buffers, rerouting, or another policy.

This is design context, not an existing repository feature. moe_forward currently groups assignments without dropping: actual assignment counts determine group_sizes, and there is no capacity-factor setting or automatic overflow dropping. That avoids this dropping semantics but not load imbalance, communication, or temporary-memory costs. Switch Transformer is a primary reference for capacity and balancing choices.

To encourage distributed assignments, code computes average routing probability \(\bar p_e\) and assignment frequency \(\rho_e\). With all tokens valid,

\[ \bar p_e=\frac1{T_{\rm tok}}\sum_t p_{t,e},\qquad \rho_e=\frac{\#\{\text{assignments to }e\}} {T_{\rm tok}k_{\rm sel}},\qquad \mathcal L_{\rm aux}=n_{\rm exp}\sum_e \bar p_e\,\operatorname{stopgrad}(\rho_e). \]

With a mask, numerator and denominator use valid-token weights. Our four-token example has \(\bar p=(0.55,0.45)\) and \(\rho=(0.5,0.5)\), giving \(\mathcal L_{\rm aux}=1\). If every token instead has probabilities \((0.9,0.1)\) and top-1 chooses \(E_1\), the value is \(2\times0.9=1.8\). This shows a different signal for concentrated load. It does not prove that 1 is a universal lower bound, and it is not a language-model accuracy score.

Code also computes \(\mathcal L_z=T_{\rm tok}^{-1}\sum_t(\log\sum_e e^{r_{t,e}})^2\), again mask-weighted when appropriate, to control router-logit scale. Training adds auxiliary and z-loss terms according to configuration. Report NLL separately when discussing language-model quality; changing a regularization coefficient is not itself an improvement in prediction.

docs.title: Why group the matrix multiplications
docs.text:
Calling an MLP separately for every routed token creates many small matrix multiplications that may underuse the GPU. Grouped computation places inputs for the same expert together and applies that expert's matrices. For our four tokens, the logical operations include

\[ \begin{bmatrix}h_0\\h_2\end{bmatrix}W_1,\qquad \begin{bmatrix}h_1\\h_3\end{bmatrix}W_2. \]

Grouped GEMM describes several input groups multiplied by their respective weights. It does not merge experts into an ordinary dense layer. moe.py stably sorts expert IDs, constructs token indices and group sizes, computes SwiGLU gate/up/down projections, and scatters results back before weighting them. The order \([0,2,1,3]\) is a minimal case that can be checked by hand.

However, using grouped GEMM does not establish that higher-order training computes only selected experts' FLOPs. The ordinary primal forward in grouped_gemm.py uses jax.lax.ragged_dot. Its custom JVP supports batching and higher derivatives through a reference path that loops over experts and combines results with masks. The opening active-parameter estimate describes algorithmic structure; actual inner/outer-loop training cost needs compiled cost analysis and device measurements. This matters for the next chapter's compute-matched comparisons.

docs.title: Where the experts live on two GPUs
docs.text:
The tiny mesh validation has four experts with \(d=d_{\rm ff}=16\). Under code's weight storage convention, one gate-weight tensor has global shape \([4,16,16]\): expert, output, input. With two GPUs and expert_parallel_size=2:

Object Global shape GPU 0 local shape GPU 1 local shape Expert gate weights \([4,16,16]\) \([2,16,16]\) \([2,16,16]\) Validation token IDs \([2,5]\) \([2,5]\) \([2,5]\) Prediction mask \([2,4]\) \([2,4]\) \([2,4]\)

The mesh is \(\text{data}=1,\text{expert}=2\), so inputs are not split again along data. Five tokens supply four next-token targets, extending the preceding chapter's alignment to distributed inputs. JAX arranges transfers according to sharding and the computation graph. There is no single handwritten all-to-all call in this code that accounts for all communication; inspect compiled execution or a profiler for actual collectives.

After installing the environment, run from the repository root with exactly two GPUs visible to the remote job. The script places all visible devices in its mesh: eight visible GPUs produce data=4, expert=2, which cannot partition the built-in batch of 2. Request a two-GPU allocation or select two devices within the scheduler's allocated mapping; do not overwrite that mapping with machine-global GPU indices.

bash scripts/validate_mesh.sh \
  outputs/ch19/mesh.json \
  outputs/ch19/checkpoints

The expected report contains passed: true, scale: "tiny", mesh, expert_shards, and checkpoint_roundtrip: true. With exactly two GPUs, expect data=1 and expert=2, with global expert dimension 4 and local expert dimension 2. The script runs two training steps; in tiny mode, it restores model and optimizer state and compares the subsequent training step.

If the device count is not divisible by expert parallelism, inspect visible devices and mesh settings first. If expert matrices cannot be partitioned, inspect expert count and partition axes. For restoration failures, inspect the checkpoint directory and original error instead of bypassing the check. Success covers this short sequence, precision, and topology; it does not establish large-model load balance, communication efficiency, or long-run quality gains.

docs.title: Separate the research questions
docs.text:
moe.py also allows fast-router corrections or Delta-memory reads to modify logits, and shared-expert outputs to join the residual stream. Distinguish the three adaptation routes: mlp updates the additional dense MLP-prime before MoE, router updates a routing adapter, and delta_router modifies routing through recurrent memory state. The current inner loop does not update moe.experts; expert parameters are trained by the outer loop.

These switches alter adaptation location or state mechanisms. Enabling all of them at once does not support a clear claim that “MoE is better.” Start with grouping and restoration in ordinary MoE, then separately compare dense MLP-prime adaptation, routing-adapter updates, memory routing, and repeated shared-parameter computation.

The evidence chain is now concrete: scores determine selections, selections determine assignments, assignments determine groups, and grouped results return to token outputs. Measure load and cost along that same chain. The next chapter puts those costs alongside model quality.

docs.title: 20. Ablations, cost, and scaling: attributing an improvement
From completing a run to answering a question
docs.text:
Suppose two jobs finish with validation NLLs of 2.10 for A and 1.98 for B. Is B's architecture better? Not yet: B might have seen more data, used a different tokenizer, or taken twice as long. An experiment needs an attributable question before it needs a result.

We place the previous chapters' implementations inside a comparison protocol. The central question is how much quality changes when the same architecture enables test-time updates, and what that change costs. We define controls, calculate a quality–cost table, and then distinguish the evidence supplied by configuration generation, profiling, and scaling fits. The mathematics needed is means, variance, and power functions, explained in context.

Figure 6. Closing the experimental loop. Follow the question through configuration, execution, evidence, and judgment. Every conclusion should lead back to the configuration and measurement that produced it, not just an experiment name.

docs.title: Decide which one thing changes
docs.text:
In the C2/F2 (or C4/F4) comparison, both arms retain the same fast-MLP architecture and initial parameters; only inner-loop updating changes. The number identifies the full-attention layer count. This asks whether adaptation helps. Removing MLP-prime from the C arm changes both parameter count and the forward function. That asks about the combined effect of extra structure and adaptation, and cannot attribute the whole difference to updating.

Write the protocol before launching training. “The same” should identify concrete files and hashes, not merely say that both runs use a similarly named dataset.

Item Constraint for an update ablation Why it matters Tokenizer, vocabulary, special tokens Same versions and files Define the prediction task and token count Split, cleaning, packing, mask Same manifest and sampling rules Define the distribution actually observed Architecture, initialization, precision Same configuration and paired seed Control capacity and starting point Batch, learning rate, optimizer, schedule Same unless explicitly studied Control optimization Inner-update switch The deliberately changed variable Define the treatment Evaluation text, context, state reset Same and documented Control advantages from evaluation state

Matching initialization does not imply matching the entire training trajectory. Updates change outer-loop gradients, so later static parameters can diverge. We control the starting point and protocol, not force the final weights to match. Evaluation must also specify whether fast state crosses document boundaries: reset single-document performance and continuous-stream adaptation answer different questions.

Structural ablations can follow: removing the fast MLP, changing suffix depth, modifying attention layout, enabling MoE, or repeating blocks. Recount parameters and cost for every change; a “125M” recipe label is not an exact parameter measurement.

docs.title: Calculate quality and cost together
docs.text:
The following numbers are hypothetical teaching values, not repository results. Both arms have 128M parameters and process the same \(D_{\rm valid}=1{,}000{,}000\) valid target tokens. Times exclude compilation and data preparation.

Arm Inner updates Validation NLL Steady training valid tokens/s Training time Peak memory C Off 2.10 20,000 50.0 s 10 GiB F On 1.98 12,000 83.3 s 13 GiB

Time is \(t=D_{\rm valid}/r\), so \(1{,}000{,}000/12{,}000\approx83.3\) seconds. With the same tokenizer and evaluation targets, NLL improves by \(0.12\) nat/token, corresponding to perplexity ratio \(e^{-0.12}\approx0.887\). F's time per token is \(20{,}000/12{,}000\approx1.67\) times C's. The table supports a quality gain with increased cost under a fixed-token budget.

Under a fixed 50-second budget, C processes one million valid tokens while F processes about 600,000. The NLL of 1.98 belongs to F after one million tokens; it cannot be assigned to the earlier 600,000-token checkpoint. A time-matched claim requires evaluating that checkpoint. If the objective is reaching a target NLL, compare when each learning curve first reaches the threshold instead of comparing final points alone.

Valid-token count is \(D_{\rm valid}=\sum_{k,b,t}m_{k,b,t}\), not simply steps times batch times length. Padding, document-boundary exclusions, and other masks can make those counts differ. Record both scheduled positions and supervised targets to explain why 100 steps need not contain equal training information. Per-token NLL across different tokenizers is also not directly comparable; hold the task fixed or add a metric normalized by a common raw-text unit.

For a training-FLOP budget, let valid-token costs be \(f_C,f_F\). Matching compute requires \(D_Cf_C\approx D_Ff_F\). Those costs must correspond to actual inner updates, higher derivatives, sequence lengths, and precision. A generic \(6ND\) dense-training estimate does not automatically cover TTT trajectories, the MoE derivative reference path, or long-context attention overhead.

docs.title: Why one seed is insufficient
docs.text:
Initialization, data order, and execution can introduce variation. Pair C and F by seed to reduce unrelated differences, then analyze each pair's difference. Suppose three paired seeds produce NLL differences \(-0.10,-0.12,-0.08\), again hypothetical:

\[ \bar\delta=-0.10,\qquad s=\sqrt{\frac{(0)^2+(-0.02)^2+(0.02)^2}{3-1}}=0.02,\qquad \operatorname{SE}(\bar\delta)=\frac{s}{\sqrt3}\approx0.0115. \]

The mean describes observed improvement; sample standard deviation describes seed variation; standard error describes uncertainty in the estimated mean under assumptions such as approximately independent repetitions. Three seeds do not establish stability across all domains or scales. Do not draw an unexplained “95% confidence interval” from them, or treat token positions as independent training runs.

Keep per-seed results, failed jobs, and exclusion reasons. Selecting favorable seeds after seeing outcomes changes the question answered by any subsequent average.

docs.title: Generate configurations and inspect the result
docs.text:
ttt/experiments.py generates dense, hybrid, TTT, and optional MoE/Loop ablations. On a remote machine with the environment installed, run from the repository root:

.venv/bin/python -m ttt.experiments \
  --output outputs/ch20/configs \
  --sizes 125m \
  --tokens 1000000 \
  --include-moe

Expect outputs/ch20/configs/manifest.json and experiment JSON files under 125m/. Standard output also prints the manifest. Inspect experiment paths, scheduled_tokens, and pending compute-matched arms awaiting cost measurements. Rounding steps upward can schedule slightly more than one million positions; this is also not the masked valid-target count.

This command generates configurations. It does not train, download a tokenizer, or prepare data. The recipe references a Llama tokenizer; training still requires checking access, actual tokenizer files, and vocabulary alignment. If output is missing, inspect argument errors and directory permissions first. If compute-matched arms remain pending, provide cost records instead of manually declaring completion. Configuration generation does not prove trainability or matched compute.

Cost input records training_flops_per_token by experiment name and labels method as profiler or xla_estimate. The generator adjusts baseline steps using the ratio of per-token costs. Measurements must match the corresponding configurations; tiny-model costs cannot be substituted for 125M-model costs.

docs.title: Distinguish inference profiling from training-cost estimates
docs.text:
A successful tiny mesh validation in the preceding chapter leaves the real checkpoint outputs/ch19/checkpoints/mesh-step-2.orbax. This command uses it with context plus decoding length \(8+4=12\), below its maximum position 16:

JAX_PLATFORMS=cuda .venv/bin/python -m ttt.profile \
  --checkpoint outputs/ch19/checkpoints/mesh-step-2.orbax \
  --context-length 8 \
  --decode-tokens 4 \
  --training-flops

Standard output is JSON containing parameters, prefill_seconds, decode_seconds, decode_tokens_per_second, state_bytes, and inner_updates. Additional training-estimate fields are xla_estimated_training_flops and xla_estimated_flops_per_token. The command does not write a default report file; redirect output into the experiment directory and retain the command and environment when recording a measurement.

profile_session performs one full warmup run and then one measured run, waiting for device results before reading timings. It measures single-session prefill and token-by-token decode, not training tokens/s or concurrent serving throughput. device_peak_bytes comes from device statistics, can be absent, and is a process-level peak rather than memory uniquely added by this measurement. parameters.fast_mlp counts the initial fast-state subtree, already included in total; do not add it twice.

Training FLOPs come from compiled graph cost analysis, not hardware counters. They do not include the entire input pipeline, optimizer, and checkpoint overhead; unavailable backend statistics can produce null. If the checkpoint is missing, complete the previous validation first. If lengths fail, inspect the saved configuration. If estimates are unavailable, retain that fact rather than inserting zero. When graphs differ substantially, report estimates together with measured training time.

docs.title: A scaling hypothesis must face held-out scales
docs.text:
A result at one size does not automatically extrapolate. An empirical model can express loss as a function of parameters \(N\) and training targets \(D\). ttt/scaling.py uses normalized variables:

\[ \widehat{\mathcal L}(N,D) =L_\infty+ A\left(\frac{N}{10^6}\right)^{-\alpha} +B_s\left(\frac{D}{10^9}\right)^{-\beta}. \]

\(L_\infty\) is the fitted floor term; \(A,B_s\) set scales; \(\alpha,\beta\) describe rates of decrease. The subscript separates coefficient \(B_s\) from batch size \(B\); JSON retains the code's keys E, A, and B. Doubling \(N\) multiplies the parameter term by \(2^{-\alpha}\); it does not necessarily halve total loss. This is an empirical fit to a fixed protocol, not a theorem covering every architecture.

The fitter requires at least eight training results, three distinct parameter counts, and three distinct token counts. Each input row provides parameters, tokens, and loss; held_out: true excludes a scale from fitting. The guard checks counts and distinct values. Researchers must still design crossed coverage so that “larger models always train longer” does not confound the two effects.

Output includes training RMSE, held-out predictions, and bootstrap intervals. Small training error does not establish reliable extrapolation. Resampling existing observations does not automatically include contamination, implementation errors, or model misspecification. Reserve scales first, fit second, and inspect held-out error third. Repeatedly choosing formulas to match the held-out points requires a new final validation set.

A set of configuration files is not a research conclusion. Quality, cost, repeated runs, and held-out scales must support that conclusion together. The next chapter turns this principle into explicit admission criteria for larger training.

docs.title: 21. GPUs, multiple devices, and checkpoints: when to scale a run
Three kinds of success require three kinds of evidence
docs.text:
A tiny model producing finite GPU loss establishes that one small graph runs. It does not establish intended parameter partitioning, continuation after interruption, or sufficient memory for the target length and batch. Before scaling, identify which admission criteria have actually been met.

We retain the tiny model and two-device expert example, separating numerical correctness, distributed-state correctness, and target-configuration readiness. Prerequisites are tensor shapes, inner/outer loops, and checkpoint purpose. We begin with a concrete two-GPU shape table rather than assuming familiarity with device meshes.

Level Question Current main entry point Small-configuration functionality Finite gradients, causality, batch/streaming agreement? scripts/validate_gpu.sh Distributed state Sharded training and the next step after restore agree? Tiny mode of scripts/validate_mesh.sh Production-run admission Target memory, sustained throughput, recovery capability? Target-configuration trials and separate evidence

The final row is an experimental admission policy, not an existing one-command certification. We distinguish current report fields from measurements still required on target hardware.

docs.title: Start with single-GPU functionality
docs.text:
After environment installation and GPU allocation on a remote node, run from the repository root:

bash scripts/validate_gpu.sh outputs/ch21/gpu-validation.json

The script explicitly requires the CUDA backend, writes outputs/ch21/environment.json, and runs ttt.validate. A successful report contains top-level passed: true, environment, and cases. Cases include dense, gdn, MoE adaptation variants, repeated-computation variants, and context lengths 64 and 512 by default. Here dense means the case does not use MoE; it does not mean fast MLPs or TTT updates are disabled.

Each case mainly checks three properties. First, sequence loss and every gradient leaf are finite. Second, streaming logits differ from the chunked training reference by at most \(10^{-3}\) in maximum absolute error. Third, changing second-half inputs preserves first-half logits under atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-4. The third check is an assertion, not a separate causality boolean in the JSON.

These thresholds belong to the current float32 tiny cases, not every precision and scale. Failure reports include passed: false, error_type, error, and environment information. For missing GPUs, inspect JAX/CUDA setup. For nonfinite values, inspect precision, learning rates, and clipping. For streaming or causal differences, inspect target shifts, update boundaries, and caches. Retain stderr: the JSON summary does not contain the complete traceback.

Success does not validate 32K or 128K context: default context cases are only 64 and 512. It does not run session snapshot restoration, real-data cleaning checks, or validation-set quality evaluation. Record the cases, lengths, and dtype with the report.

docs.title: Compilation and execution are different timing boundaries
docs.text:
JAX's first execution can require compiling a Python-described graph into a device program. Later calls with the same shapes and types usually reuse it. Shape changes can trigger new compilation. At minimum, distinguish compilation, sustained execution, and end-to-end time including input/output.

Single-GPU validation explicitly calls lower(...).compile() and records compilation_seconds. It then executes one compiled loss-and-gradient computation, waits for the result, and records training_seconds. That is one graph execution, not a multi-sample steady training mean. It also excludes the complete optimizer update and data input.

Consider hypothetical compilation of 35 seconds followed by ten one-second steps, each containing 2048 valid targets. Execution-only throughput is \(20{,}480/10=2048\) tokens/s; including compilation, the short job averages \(20{,}480/45\approx455.1\) tokens/s. Both are reportable with their boundaries. The latter does not isolate steady kernel efficiency; the former does not capture short-job startup cost.

A proper measurement warms up the target shapes and times several consecutive training steps, waiting for asynchronous device work at timing boundaries. Record valid-token counts, the step-time distribution, inclusion of data waits and checkpoints, device count, and peak memory. Without synchronization, a timer may measure host submission instead of device execution. Current validation scripts do not supply this complete steady-state distribution; renaming one field does not create the evidence.

docs.title: Two GPUs must fit the mesh dimensions
docs.text:
A mesh arranges devices along named axes such as data and expert. create_mesh reshapes the global device array to [data, expert], so

\[ n_{\rm devices}=n_{\rm data}\,n_{\rm expert}. \]

Two GPUs can form \((2,1)\) or \((1,2)\). A \((2,2)\) mesh requires four GPUs; two devices cannot simultaneously provide independent two-way data and two-way expert axes.

Two-GPU topology data expert Conceptual input distribution for global hidden \([8,16,16]\) Actual parameter partition for four-expert weights \([4,16,16]\) Distribute samples along data 2 1 \([4,16,16]\) per device \([4,8,16]\) per device with default parameter sharding Distribute experts along expert 1 2 Input \([8,16,16]\) on each device \([2,16,16]\) per device

The first row matters: default shard_parameters=True can partition expert matrices' second dimension along data. This is not pure data parallelism with all parameters replicated. Nonexpert matrices can also partition their first dimension along data. The hidden column illustrates sample distribution, not a guarantee for every intermediate activation. Inspect tree_shardings and actual shards to establish a parameter's placement.

Global batch must be divisible by \(n_{\rm data}\), and expert count must be divisible by \(n_{\rm expert}\). Checking these integer constraints first is usually more useful than changing batch sizes blindly after a communication failure.

docs.title: What the two-device restore check actually covers
docs.text:
Run the following in a remote job with exactly two visible GPUs. Use a new output directory for a repeat audit and retain earlier reports and checkpoints. The default mesh uses all visible devices; eight GPUs produce data=4, expert=2, incompatible with the built-in batch of 2. Request two GPUs or select two devices within the scheduler's allocated mapping; do not replace it with machine-global GPU indices.

bash scripts/validate_mesh.sh \
  outputs/ch21/mesh-validation.json \
  outputs/ch21/mesh-checkpoints

The default is expert_parallel_size=2. With exactly two devices, expect data=1 and expert=2, and expert_shards showing global expert dimension 4 and local dimension 2. The report also includes two step_seconds, corresponding metrics, device_memory, and checkpoint_roundtrip: true in tiny mode.

The script trains two steps, saves mesh-step-2.orbax, restores model, optimizer, and step, and compares local arrays. It then takes one further step from the original and restored states and compares parameters, optimizer state, and loss. Merely opening a file is much weaker: omitting Adam momentum can still produce a loadable checkpoint that follows a different trajectory.

The batch is two fixed short sequences. This restore check does not cover real data cursors, process termination mid-run, filesystem failures, or changing the device topology. Training recovery in ttt/train.py additionally restores sampling state; session recovery from the preceding chapter is another kind of state. These are not interchangeable meanings of “checkpoint passed.”

For divisibility failures, inspect mesh and shapes. For write failures, inspect existing checkpoint names, storage, and permissions. For next-step differences, inspect optimizer state, step, and precision; retain discrepancies instead of simply loosening equality checks. The first reported step includes compilation, and the second is one execution. They do not establish a sustained step-time distribution.

docs.title: A parameter-scale trial has limits too
docs.text:
ttt.validate_mesh also accepts --scale 1b. For this worked two-device example, keep exactly two visible GPUs. Its built-in batch of 2 also constrains other topologies: four devices give data=2 and divide the batch, whereas eight devices give data=4 and do not. Consider this larger parameter trial only after tiny validation and with enough target-device memory. It is not the minimum required checkpoint for this chapter:

JAX_PLATFORMS=cuda .venv/bin/python -m ttt.validate_mesh \
  --scale 1b \
  --expert-parallel-size 2 \
  --require-gpu \
  --output outputs/ch21/mesh-1b.json

Expected JSON has scale: "1b", a measured parameters count, and finite metrics for two steps. To avoid writing a large extra checkpoint, this mode skips restoration, so checkpoint_roundtrip should be false. The scale name is a recipe tier, not a substitute for counting parameters.

Its position limit is only 16, and training sequence length is 4. It probes larger parameter and sharding execution, not 1B long-context pretraining reproduction. For OOM, inspect actual parameters, precision, sharding, and current memory occupancy; remember that this trial already uses a very short sequence. Success still leaves target length, target batch, data throughput, and large-checkpoint recovery unverified.

docs.title: Admission criteria for a substantial training run
docs.text:
Retain the following as a manual experiment review. These are not additional fields emitted by the current scripts. Missing evidence should be marked unverified, not inferred from tiny passed.

Criterion Evidence needed Why scaling without it is premature Consistent data and task Manifest, tokenizer hashes, masks, valid-target statistics The job may train a different task or contaminate evaluation Causal and numerical correctness Relevant finite-gradient, streaming, and future-perturbation checks More compute amplifies implementation mistakes Target configuration fits Measured memory and headroom at target length, batch, precision Tiny runs do not predict activation peaks Sustained stability Warmed-up step-time distribution, loss/gradient trends, valid tokens/s One execution misses intermittent stalls or divergence Training recovery Model, optimizer, step, data cursor, and next-step comparison Restore can silently change the data or optimization trajectory Accounted cost Compilation, training, data waits, saving, device-hours Budget-matched comparisons become impossible Traceable provenance Commit, environment, command, configuration, logs, failures Another machine cannot explain discrepancies

Choose thresholds before the run, including memory headroom, acceptable numerical error, and measurement duration. There is no universal numeric threshold suitable for every device. On failure, keep the original error together with its triggering configuration and report. Script-provided error JSON is a starting point; stage attribution and repair evidence still need to be recorded.

“Ready to scale” is now a set of inspectable conditions rather than an absence of exceptions. Only then should the real corpus from the data chapters enter larger training, evaluated with the preceding chapter's quality–cost protocol.

docs.title: 4. Pretraining Data: Distribution, Quality, and Reproducibility
Why data is the first design decision
docs.text:
Pretraining is not a matter of putting a pile of text on a GPU and waiting for the model to absorb “the internet.” The model only sees the training windows produced by the data pipeline. Source selection, filtering, deduplication, tokenization, packing, and masking together define what the optimizer is asked to learn. Data is therefore part of the model specification, rather than a directory chosen after the architecture.

Data changes the result in at least three ways:

  • Capability coverage. Web pages, code, books, papers, and conversations contain different vocabularies, structures, and tasks. Their mixture changes coverage of knowledge, long context, programming syntax, and languages.
  • Training cost. Different tokenizers produce different token counts for the same text. Longer sequences also increase activation, attention, and KV-cache costs. Cleaning and deduplication determine how much distinct content fits within a fixed token budget.
  • Evaluation validity. If validation contains near duplicates of training, a low validation loss may measure memorization. If filtering removes a class of text, the evaluation no longer represents the intended users. Splitting is part of the evaluation protocol.

This small example shows why file counts do not describe the training distribution:

Source Documents Mean tokens Share after direct token concatenation Possible bias Web 900,000 1,000 about 82% broad coverage, with templates and noise Code 50,000 2,000 about 9% concentrated syntax and tool-use examples Books 10,000 10,000 about 9% richer long-form structure, fewer documents

docs.title: Overview: trace one short text first
docs.text:
This chapter starts with a short running example rather than a large download. We follow “The cat sits.” from a raw record through cleaning, a token stream, a training window, and one loss term. By the end, you should be able to explain why a token enters the loss denominator and run a tiny sharded dataset with a manifest.

Suppose the raw collection has two records: record \(r_1\) contains “The cat sits.” and record \(r_2\) is a web mirror. If cleaning and deduplication keep only \(r_1\), uniform sampling changes from \(P(r_1)=P(r_2)=1/2\) to \(P(r_1)=1\). The file name did not change; the distribution seen by the model did.

To isolate the shift rule, use the invented short sequence \(s=(10,11,12,2)\), with 2 as EOS. These are not the actual byte-tokenizer IDs of the sentence above; we compute real encodings in the tokenizer chapter. A length-3 window becomes \(X=(10,11,12)\), \(Y=(11,12,2)\), and \(M=(1,1,1)\). Inputs and targets differ by one position, connecting a document to the summands in cross-entropy.

The command below encodes the repository JSONL example into shards and writes a manifest. This is data generation; the Dataset and preflight chapters separately check that the loader can read it correctly. Generation alone establishes neither cleaning quality, contamination checks, nor model generalization.

.venv/bin/python -m ttt.data \
  --input examples/sample.jsonl \
  --output outputs/book-data-contract \
  --sharded --tokenizer byte --shard-tokens 256

On success, outputs/book-data-contract/manifest.json and token/mask shards should exist. On failure, check the input path, vocabulary size, and write permission first. The next sections explain how acquisition, cleaning, deduplication, and splitting change this chain.

Direct concatenation makes web tokens dominate; source-uniform sampling gives a different distribution. Both are implementable, but they optimize different objectives. If 30% of web text is duplicated templates, cleaning lowers its effective token count and automatically increases the relative weight of code and books unless the mixture is recomputed. Later sections turn this example into an explicit, reproducible sampling protocol.

Figure 2. The data pipeline. The data chapter treats training as an auditable chain from raw records to \(X,Y,M\) and the loss.

docs.title: What is a tokenizer? Turning text into model-readable tokens
docs.text:
A model cannot consume Unicode text directly. A tokenizer is a rule or learned model that encodes text as an integer sequence: it maps a text string \(u\) to tokens \(s\), then maps each token to an ID in a fixed vocabulary. A token need not be a complete word; it may be a byte, character, or subword. The ID is an index, so its numeric value does not express semantic similarity.

The conversion can be written as

\[ u \xrightarrow{\ \tau\ } s=(s_1,\ldots,s_L), \qquad s_t\in\{0,\ldots,V-1\}, \]

where \(\tau\) is the tokenizer, \(V\) is the vocabulary size, and \(L\) is the number of tokens produced for this text. The model's embedding looks up rows from this vocabulary, and the final classification head maps a hidden vector back to the same \(V\) possible next-token IDs. Replacing the tokenizer can therefore change sequence length, the number of training positions, memory cost, and the output-head dimension at the same time.

A tokenizer also defines special-token semantics, such as EOS for a document boundary, BOS for a sequence start, PAD for alignment, and unknown or byte-fallback behavior. These choices affect document boundaries, packing, loss masks, and evaluation, so a tokenizer is part of the data protocol rather than a preprocessing script that can be swapped in at the end. A reproducible run records at least the tokenizer file or model name, revision, vocabulary size, special-token IDs, and normalization rules. Changing any of them requires regenerating token shards and updating the manifest. Chapter 9 covers tokenizer training, vocabulary selection, and efficiency measurements.

docs.title: Turn the motivation into a measurable distribution
docs.text:
We now define two objects that are often left implicit: the training data distribution and the prediction loss. Cleaning, tokenization, packing, and manifests only fit together once these objects are explicit. Following the book-wide notation, a tokenized document stream is \(s\), an input token is \(x\), a next-token target is \(y\), and model parameters are \(\theta\).

Let one raw record be

\[ r_i=(u_i,m_i), \]

where \(u_i\) is text and \(m_i\) contains metadata such as source, license, language, time, and document group. Let \(P_{\mathrm{raw}}\) denote the distribution of raw records. For a fixed collection of raw files, the simplest uniform-sampling case is:

If we sample uniformly from \(N\) raw records, then

\[ P_{\mathrm{raw}}(r_i)=\frac{1}{N}. \]

For two records \(r_1\) and \(r_2\), each has probability \(1/2\). A collection of raw files is not yet the final training distribution. After source selection, cleaning, deduplication, and splitting, we obtain a training collection

\[ C_{\mathrm{train}}=\{r_1,\ldots,r_n\}. \]

Cleaning can modify text or reject a record. Rejection requires renormalizing probabilities: after dropping one of three equally likely records, each survivor has probability \(1/2\), not \(1/3\). Deduplication also compares records, so it is not simply a transformation applied independently to each text. We therefore first fix the cleaned, deduplicated training split and then define how to sample it.
