Assign each surviving record a nonnegative weight \(w_i\), with at least one positive weight. The document sampling distribution is

\[ P_{\mathrm{doc}}(r_i)= \frac{w_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_j}. \]

Uniform document sampling, length-weighted sampling, and source-level sampling therefore define different distributions. The number of files alone does not say what the model sees.

Document distribution and training-position distribution are also different objects. Uniformly selecting documents can still give longer documents more loss positions. Sampling token starts uniformly produces another weighting over short documents, long documents, and boundaries. Document count, token count, and supervised loss positions are not interchangeable statistics.

A tokenizer \(\tau\) maps document text to a token sequence:

\[ \tau(u_i)=s^{(i)}=(s^{(i)}_1,\ldots,s^{(i)}_{L_i}), \qquad s^{(i)}_t\in\{0,\ldots,V-1\}, \]

where \(V\) is the vocabulary size. We must next decide whether to sample inside one document or inside a concatenated stream. If we first select a document and then sample a window within it, call the second step's conditional distribution \(P_\Pi\). Summing over possible documents gives

\[ P_{\mathrm{win}}(X,Y,M) = \sum_i P_{\mathrm{doc}}(r_i) \,P_{\Pi}(X,Y,M\mid \tau(u_i)). \]

The repository instead concatenates encoded documents into a fixed stream \(S=(S_1,\ldots,S_T)\), accompanied by a mask stream. A prediction window of length \(L\) needs \(L+1\) consecutive tokens, so its valid starts are \(a=1,\ldots,T-L\). Write \(W_a=(X_a,Y_a,M_a)\) for the shifted window at start \(a\). Uniformly sampling starts gives

\[ P_{\mathrm{win}}(W) =\frac{1}{T-L}\sum_{a=1}^{T-L}\mathbf{1}\{W_a=W\}. \]

The indicator \(\mathbf{1}\) is 1 when its condition holds and 0 otherwise. If two starts produce identical windows, both count. This expression includes windows crossing document boundaries; the preceding document-local formula does not. Document order, EOS, BOS, window length, and masks can all change \(P_{\mathrm{win}}\).

docs.title: What exactly is prediction loss?
docs.text:
Let a training window contain the consecutive token stream

\[ s=(s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_{L+1}). \]

A causal language model uses the token at each position as input and the following token as target:

\[ x_t=s_t,\qquad y_t=s_{t+1}, \qquad X=(x_1,\ldots,x_L),\quad Y=(y_1,\ldots,y_L). \]

For model parameters \(\theta\), the loss at position \(t\) is the negative log probability assigned to the observed target token:

\[ \ell_t(\theta)=-\log p_\theta(y_t\mid x_{1:t}). \]

If the model emits logits \(\mathbf{z}_\theta(x_{1:t})\) at position \(t\), then

\[ p_\theta(v\mid x_{1:t}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_\theta(x_{1:t}))_v. \]

If \(M=(m_1,\ldots,m_L)\) is a loss mask, with \(m_t=1\) for supervised positions and \(m_t=0\) for ignored positions, the average window loss is

\[ \ell(\theta;X,Y,M) = -\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{L}m_t\log p_\theta(y_t\mid x_{1:t})} {\sum_{t=1}^{L}m_t}. \]

The preceding expression requires \(\sum_t m_t>0\). An entirely ignored window has no defined average loss and should be reported separately by data checks. We must also choose how to combine windows: one vote per window or one vote per valid token? Let \(A=\sum_t m_t\ell_t\) be a window's total loss and \(K=\sum_t m_t\) its valid count. The two objectives are

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{window}}=\mathbb{E}[A/K], \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{token}}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[A]}{\mathbb{E}[K]}. \]

They coincide under conditions such as a fixed valid count. Suppose one window has a single valid position with loss 4, while another has three valid positions with loss 1 each. Averaging window means gives \((4+1)/2=2.5\); pooling valid positions gives \((4+3)/4=1.75\). The latter gives every valid position equal weight and is the convention used here for dataset-level loss.

A finite evaluation observes \(N\) sampled windows. Its token-weighted estimator is

\[ \widehat{\mathcal{L}}_N(\theta) = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{L_k} m^{(k)}_t\ell^{(k)}_t(\theta)} {\sum_{k=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{L_k}m^{(k)}_t}. \]

Training also normalizes by valid positions within each minibatch. A random numerator divided by a random denominator is generally not an unbiased estimator of the population ratio, especially when valid counts vary substantially. To aggregate evaluation batches, sum their total losses and valid counts before dividing; do not simply average their mean losses. Gradient updates aim to reduce the chosen training objective, but one update need not reduce every window's loss.

Validation loss uses the same definition with an independent \(P_{\mathrm{val}}\) in place of \(P_{\mathrm{win}}\). Training loss asks whether the model fits the training distribution; validation loss asks how it predicts on another declared distribution. If validation contains near duplicates of training, the second question has not been measured reliably.

This is why the chapter treats data as part of the objective. Changing \(P_{\mathrm{doc}}\), \(\tau\), \(\Pi\), or \(M\) changes the target function even when architecture and optimizer remain unchanged.

docs.title: How a raw document becomes a training signal
docs.text:
The data pipeline is not just a file transfer to the GPU. It is a sequence of transformations that changes the mathematical object being optimized:

flowchart LR
    A[Raw file] --> B[Document record and metadata]
    B --> C[Clean, deduplicate, split]
    C --> D[Tokenizer: text → token IDs]
    D --> E[Packing and window sampling]
    E --> F[input_ids / labels / loss_mask]
    F --> G[Cross-entropy and gradients]
    G --> H[Parameter update]

For an illustrative token sequence:

Object Value Token stream \(s\) \((10,11,12,2)\) Teaching array input_ids (mathematical \(X\)) \((10,11,12)\) Teaching array labels (mathematical \(Y\)) \((11,12,2)\) Teaching array loss_mask (mathematical \(M\)) \((1,1,1)\)

These names explain the three mathematical objects. The actual loader returns unshifted tokens and target masks; sequence_loss constructs inputs and targets from tokens.

The window loss is

\[ -\frac{1}{3} \left[ \log p_\theta(11\mid 10) +\log p_\theta(12\mid 10,11) +\log p_\theta(2\mid 10,11,12) \right]. \]

Masking the final EOS changes both the numerator and denominator. Crossing a document boundary changes the available context. A tokenizer that produces more tokens increases the number of prediction positions and the cost. The training signal is therefore not raw text itself; it is the \((X,Y,M)\) object constructed by these rules.

docs.title: What each transformation changes
docs.text:
Source selection changes support. Web text, code, books, and papers expose different vocabularies, lengths, and structures. A model receives signal only from the regions sampled into training.

Cleaning changes the sample set. Removing navigation pages, corrupted text, and parser failures changes which records remain in \(C_{\mathrm{train}}\). Over-filtering can remove code, mathematics, minority languages, or long documents.

Deduplication changes weights. Repeating one document one hundred times increases its probability under \(P_{\mathrm{doc}}\). Near duplicates across training and validation also destroy evaluation independence.

Splitting changes the evaluation object. Document-group splits and contamination checks determine whether validation windows represent unseen content. A contaminated benchmark can turn low loss or high accuracy into memorization evidence.

Tokenization changes the sample space and cost. The same characters can produce different token sequences. Vocabulary size affects the embedding, output head, sequence length, attention, KV cache, and throughput.

Packing and masks change conditional probabilities. Cross-document packing, EOS retention, and supervised positions all change \(P_{\mathrm{win}}\) or the window loss. Packing is part of the learning protocol, not only a storage optimization.

docs.title: A concrete mixture example
docs.text:
Source Documents Average length Total tokens Web 900,000 1,000 900M Code 50,000 2,000 100M Books 10,000 10,000 100M

Concatenation gives books \(100/1100\approx9.09\%\) of tokens. Uniformly selecting a document and taking exactly one equal-length window from it instead selects books with probability \(10{,}000/960{,}000\approx1.04\%\). Uniformly selecting one of the three sources gives books \(1/3\) of selections. A sampling rule must specify how many windows are taken after selecting a document; uniform document sampling does not automatically increase the weight of long-document sources.

If 30% of web tokens are boilerplate duplicates, cleaning may reduce effective web tokens to 630M. If the mixture is not recomputed, the effective weights of code and books rise automatically. Every stage must report its own denominator rather than only a final token total.

The current BatchStream samples windows from one logical token stream. It does not implement source-level mixture scheduling. The later mixture chapter defines that capability without claiming it already exists here.

docs.title: Data specifications to settle before training
docs.text:
Before a long run, the pipeline should answer:

  1. Is the source identifiable? Can we locate the release, retrieval time, and license?
  2. Is quality explainable? Does every filter have a version, threshold, count, and sample audit?
  3. Are splits trustworthy? Are train, validation, and test separated by document or project boundary, with near-duplicate and contamination checks?
  4. Is representation consistent? Do tokenizer, special tokens, packing, label shift, and masks agree with the model configuration?
  5. Is the version recoverable? Can manifest, shard hashes, sampler state, and checkpoint identify the next batch?

Readable data is not necessarily acceptable data. Each requirement needs a saved evidence object and a later preflight check.

docs.title: Data objects and version boundaries
docs.text:
Raw files are immutable downloads or snapshots such as archives, HTML, JSONL, or repository states.

Document records contain extracted text and metadata for cleaning, deduplication, splitting, and boundary management.

Token shards contain integer sequences and supervision masks plus vocabulary, tokenizer version, dtype, shard count, and SHA256 metadata.

Training windows are fixed-length sequences sampled from the token stream and converted into input_ids, labels, loss_mask, and position state.

These objects must not share one vague “data version”. A fixed raw file can produce a new document version after cleaning changes; a fixed document set can produce a new token version after tokenizer changes; fixed shards can produce a new window protocol after sequence length or packing changes.

docs.title: What the repository currently implements
docs.text:
ttt/data.py provides a byte tokenizer and JSONL-to-token conversion. It can write one-dimensional NPY data or sharded token and mask files with a manifest.

ttt/dataset.py validates manifest version, vocab_size, paths, SHA256, token ranges, mask shapes, and mask values, then reads shards with memory mapping. BatchStream uses a NumPy generator to sample windows and stores RNG state, data digest, sequence length, batch size, and seed.

.venv/bin/python -m ttt.data \
  --input examples/sample.jsonl \
  --output outputs/book-data \
  --sharded \
  --tokenizer byte \
  --shard-tokens 256

shard-tokens is a storage-shard size, not the model sequence length. The current window can cross EOS and document boundaries, and the model has no general “reset attention at EOS” interface. The current loader should therefore be described as continuous-stream packing rather than document-isolated packing.

The manifest also lacks a complete document-offset sidecar, so arbitrary token-to-document tracing remains a requirement for a larger data pipeline. Separating implemented behavior from design requirements is part of the data standard.

docs.title: The route through the remaining data chapters
docs.text:
• 11_data_acquisition.md: source versions, licenses, downloads, and provenance;
  • 12_data_cleaning.md: normalization, format, language, length, and quality filters;
  • 13_deduplication.md: exact/near deduplication and its effect on sampling weights;
  • 14_split_and_contamination.md: train, validation, test, and contamination boundaries;
  • 15_tokenizer.md: tokenizer, vocabulary, and parameter dimensions;
  • 16_packing_and_masks.md: packing, label shift, document boundaries, and loss masks;
  • 17_dataset_and_manifest.md: shards, manifests, mmap, and recoverable sampling;
  • 18_data_mixture.md: source mixtures and deterministic sampling;
  • 19_data_preflight.md: hard gates before training;
  • 20_baseline_model.md: whether these inputs actually support learning in a dense causal model.

From the next chapter onward, “data” is no longer a vague input name. We trace each object, how it changes the training distribution, and which evidence allows the next run to check it.

docs.title: 5. Acquiring data and preserving provenance
The experiment begins before model training
docs.text:
Two students use the same download URL, training code, and random seed, but obtain different validation losses. Eventually they discover that the publisher replaced the archive between their downloads. Both files are called corpus.jsonl.gz. Their documents differ. Nothing in the model implementation had to change for the experiment to change.

The previous chapter explained why the data distribution matters. This chapter asks how to turn “these are the data we used” into a statement someone else can check. A download command alone is insufficient. We need to retain the received objects, identify their source and version, and preserve the connection between those objects and the eventual training input.

Think of receiving a laboratory sample. A label helps locate it, a batch number identifies its provenance, and a measurement checks its contents. In a data pipeline, the URL is a location, the release describes an upstream publication, and a digest helps compare the received bytes. Each answers a different question.

We begin with four original records already included in the repository. You can inspect every line without downloading an external corpus. The experiment demonstrates file identity and provenance records; it does not represent a corpus that has already passed a licensing or quality review.

docs.title: File bytes and document records are different objects
docs.text:
A file is a sequence of bytes. Each byte contains eight binary digits and can represent an integer from 0 to 255. An encoding such as UTF-8 maps text to bytes. A format such as JSON describes how text represents fields and values. These two layers explain why identical records need not have identical file bytes.

Consider two JSON representations:

{"id":"d1","text":"A cat."}
{"id": "d1", "text": "A cat."}

Saved separately, they contain different bytes because the spaces differ. A JSON parser produces the same id and text fields from both. Parsing means interpreting a format to construct program objects such as dictionaries, lists, or numbers. It does not judge whether the text is useful.

Parsing also needs an ambiguity policy. For {"text":"first text","text":"second text"}, Python keeps only the last value by default. Our acquisition reader instead rejects repeated field names within any object, including nested metadata. This differs from checking document IDs across the file: it prevents a parser's last-value rule from silently deciding which source text exists. See Python's repeated-name behavior.

JSONL places one JSON object on each nonempty physical line. A newline inside the text field is represented by the JSON escape \n, rather than arbitrarily splitting the object across lines. Our teaching parser permits blank lines and skips them. Consequently, appending a blank line changes the file without adding a document. We will use this small change to separate byte identity from record identity.

Compression adds another layer. A downloaded .gz archive and the decompressed JSONL are distinct objects. Recompression can change the archive while preserving its decompressed contents. Every digest must identify the layer it describes; comparing an archive digest with a decompressed-file digest has no useful interpretation.

docs.title: What a digest establishes
docs.text:
Let \(b\) denote a file's bytes. SHA-256 maps the input to a 256-bit result:

\[ h=\operatorname{SHA256}(b). \]

We commonly display that result as 64 hexadecimal characters, each representing four bits. This short string is a digest, convenient to store in a manifest. Python provides hashlib.sha256 in its standard library; no training framework is required.

Identical bytes always produce the same digest. Therefore different digests establish that the bytes differ. The converse is not a mathematical proof: distinct inputs can have the same digest, a situation called a collision. There are more possible files than finite digest values. SHA-256 provides a practical integrity check for ordinary experiment files, while a small experiment can also compare the bytes directly.

A digest does not identify the publisher either. Receiving a file and an alleged reference digest from the same incorrect source cannot establish the source's authenticity. A verifiable publication page, fixed release, and trustworthy acquisition channel address provenance; a digest addresses content comparison.

The smallest useful implementation is:

import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

data = Path("examples/sample.jsonl").read_bytes()
print(len(data))
print(hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest())

read_bytes() reads the actual bytes, len(data) counts them, and hexdigest() returns a printable digest. Reading the complete object into memory is appropriate for this tiny file. For large files, feed successive blocks to update() and ensure that the blocks cover the same complete object; hashing does not require loading hundreds of gigabytes into memory at once.

docs.title: A local acquisition experiment that preserves its input
docs.text:
From the repository root, using the prepared environment, run:

.venv/bin/python examples/book/acquisition_walkthrough.py \
  --input examples/sample.jsonl \
  --output outputs/book-acquisition-v1

The script uses only the Python standard library. It requires neither a GPU nor model weights. It validates the input id and text fields, requires unique document IDs, and copies the original bytes to raw.jsonl. It then creates a control copy with one additional newline byte and rereads both saved objects to compute digests, parse records, and verify their contents. It does not alter the source. The default example already ends with a newline, so appending another creates a blank line. For an input without a final newline, the added byte only terminates the last line. Either case adds one byte without adding a document.

Output Contents Question it answers raw.jsonl A copy of the received bytes What object did this run actually receive? with-extra-newline.jsonl A control with one extra newline byte Must a byte change imply a record change? source-record.json Digests, sizes, record counts, and script identity How can this observation be checked?

With the repository's default input, the report should satisfy the following conditions. These are acceptance conditions derived from the input and program; obtain the complete digests from your actual output.

{
  "records": 4,
  "byte_counts_differ_by": 1,
  "same_parsed_records": true,
  "different_byte_digest": true,
  "original_preserved": true
}

same_parsed_records compares the complete object lists parsed again from the two saved files, rather than merely counting texts. Changing a document while retaining a count of four cannot pass that comparison. original_preserved comes from comparing the source and saved copy against the received bytes; the script also checks that the control contains exactly the additional newline byte. A failed check raises an error instead of producing a report that claims success.

The source_id is a local content identifier derived from the input digest. It distinguishes this experiment's input without impersonating an external dataset release. observed_at_utc records the observation time and normally changes between runs. repository_commit records the current commit in a Git checkout and is null when running from an archive without Git metadata. The script's own digest is also recorded because an uncommitted script edit is not described by the commit ID.

Reproduction therefore does not require identical timestamp fields. Compare results determined by the fixed input, processing code, and rules. The script refuses to overwrite an existing output directory. Use outputs/book-acquisition-v2 for a second run to preserve both records.

docs.title: Extending the local record to an external source inventory
docs.text:
The local experiment has established a relationship between an input object, an action, and output objects. External acquisition adds upstream facts. Keep source information and file information as two related layers.

The source layer records the publisher, canonical location, immutable revision or snapshot when available, acquisition time, and location of the terms-review evidence. The file layer records the actual objects received, their sizes and digests, and acquisition outcomes. One source may contain a thousand files; one file may combine multiple original sources. In the latter case, preserve document-level provenance instead of collapsing it into an overly broad file label.

Do not invent missing fields. If a publisher exposes only a changing latest version, record the acquisition time, received object, and verifiable publication information available then. A service's ETag can support caching under that service's documented semantics; it is not universally a SHA-256 content digest.

Our report explicitly sets terms_review to not_performed_by_this_script. Hashing does not review terms. A real project needs evidence appropriate to the particular source and intended release objects. Raw files, cleaned text, token shards, and model weights are different objects; an ambiguous “data usable” field cannot replace the relevant records. The example fields are not legal conclusions.

docs.title: Why retain the original object?
docs.text:
Let \(R\) be the raw object, \(e\) the extractor version, and \(c\) the cleaner version. The resulting documents can be written as

\[ D_{\mathrm{clean}}=C_c(E_e(R)), \]

where \(E_e\) performs extraction and \(C_c\) performs cleaning. The subscripts emphasize that changing either program can change the documents even when \(R\) is fixed.

Suppose a web page contains prose, navigation, and code blocks. An older extractor retains the prose but drops the code; a newer version restores it. Different outputs do not imply that the downloaded page changed. If only final text remains, a reader cannot locate the loss of code in the original page, extraction stage, or later filtering.

Write each processing stage to a new location and record its input digest, code and configuration versions, output digest, and counts. These records describe a processing relationship, not merely a list of final filenames. They let us trace training tokens back through cleaned documents and extracted text to the received object. Small experiments can copy files. Large projects can use immutable object storage with manifest references. The principle is traceable identity, not unconditional duplication of every intermediate byte.

docs.title: Use the correct denominator for acquisition losses
docs.text:
Consider an explicitly hypothetical acquisition. Of 1,000 requested files, 10 fail to download. Of the 990 downloaded files, 10 cannot be parsed. The remaining 980 files yield 100,000 records, of which 500 lack the text field.

Stage Input unit and count Failure or exclusion Output Download 1,000 files 10 files 990 files Parsing 990 files 10 files 980 parseable files Field validation 100,000 records 500 records 99,500 documents

It would be wrong to report “520 items removed”: the first two rows count files, whereas the last counts records. Download success is \(990/1000=99\%\). Parseability among received files is \(980/990\approx98.99\%\). Text-field completeness among parsed records is \(99500/100000=99.5\%\). Each fraction answers a different question.

Even these totals can hide bias. If all ten failed downloads belong to a small language source, that source may lose a substantial fraction of its coverage. Break down acquisition outcomes by source, language, or format. Keep accidental operational losses separate from deliberate quality filtering so that the eventual training distribution can be explained.

We can now distinguish changes to bytes, parsing, and processing rules while preserving the acquired object. The next chapter examines the text itself: which transformations merely organize its representation, which can discard information, and how to make every keep or reject decision inspectable.

docs.title: 6. Cleaning text: what to retain, what to change, and how to check
Turn “remove dirty data” into a learning objective
docs.text:
The previous chapter stored text together with its provenance. Suppose those records now contain three kinds of material: repeated website navigation, an indented Python fragment, and a sentence containing mathematical symbols. All three fit in a text file, but the same rule need not be appropriate for all of them.

首页
首页
首页

    return x + 1

Ａ＋①＝２，这些字形先保留。

The repeated Chinese word means “home page.” It probably adds little article content. Spaces in the code may determine its structure. The circled number and fullwidth characters in the final sentence may be precisely what its author wants to discuss. A combination of “remove short lines,” “remove non-English letters,” and “strip all indentation” might produce a tidy file while removing the material we wanted to teach the model.

A language model learns by repeatedly predicting the next token in training text. Retaining more of a kind of text usually gives the model more opportunities to encounter its patterns. Filtering almost all of it leaves little opportunity to learn those expressions from this corpus. Cleaning therefore has two responsibilities: reduce useless or damaged material, and control the rejection of useful material. The retention rate is a processing statistic, not a quality score.

We begin with three distinct questions: was the file decoded correctly, should its text be normalized, and should this record be retained? We then work through 13 original records included in the repository and run a standard-library-only program that produces retained records, rejected records, and an auditable report. The thresholds are deliberately small so that every decision is inspectable. They are not recommendations for a large pretraining corpus.

docs.title: Bytes in a file, text on a screen
docs.text:
A computer stores a file as bytes. A byte has 256 possible values, often written using two hexadecimal digits, such as 41. Unicode assigns code points to text elements: A, for example, has code point U+0041. UTF-8 specifies a representation of those code points as bytes. Decoding turns bytes into a Python str; encoding turns a str into bytes. One code point can occupy several UTF-8 bytes. Python Unicode HOWTO

Consider Café. Its final accented letter can be represented by a single é or by an e followed by a combining accent. The table shows representations of the same small word, not token IDs from a tokenizer vocabulary.

Representation Unicode code points UTF-8 bytes in hexadecimal Python len Cafe\u0301: e plus combining accent 0043 0061 0066 0065 0301 43 61 66 65 cc 81 5 Café: precomposed é 0043 0061 0066 00E9 43 61 66 c3 a9 4

Here \u0301 is the Python/JSON escape for a code point, not six visible characters in the actual text. Both strings normally display as the same word, but their code points and bytes differ. Python's len counts string code points. It does not count UTF-8 bytes, does not necessarily count the characters a reader perceives, and does not count model tokens. This distinction will matter for our length threshold.

If a UTF-8 file is read using an incorrect encoding, the resulting garbled text is a decoding problem. Unicode normalization neither infers the original encoding nor reliably recovers unknown content already replaced with �. Our program decodes the entire input strictly as UTF-8. Invalid bytes stop the run before cleaning outputs are created, keeping a decoding failure from silently becoming ordinary training text.

File format and content format also differ. JSONL stores one JSON value per line; our input requires each line to be an object with a text field. That text might have come from a web article or a code repository. Successfully parsing JSON does not establish that HTML article extraction succeeded. Consider:

<nav>首页　登录</nav><article><p>雨水进入河流。</p></article>

Removing the tags alone retains both the navigation, “home page / login,” and the article, “rainwater enters the river.” Article extraction must also decide which nodes belong to the article. It should preserve paragraph boundaries so that separate paragraphs do not become joined words or sentences. Our program accepts already extracted plain text. It does not parse HTML or implement an article extractor. A source containing HTML needs extraction and an assessment of its output before these text rules are applied; passing HTML to this program does not automatically perform that step.

docs.title: What NFC and NFKC actually change
docs.text:
Normalization operates on Unicode text that has already been decoded. NFC unifies canonically equivalent representations in composed form, for example replacing e plus a combining accent with é. NFKC additionally uses compatibility equivalence and therefore removes more distinctions. Python provides these operations through unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text) and unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text). Python unicodedata

Original NFC result NFKC result Distinction to inspect Cafe\u0301 Café Café The accented letter changes from two code points to one Ａ (U+FF21) Ａ A (U+0041) The fullwidth distinction disappears ① (U+2460) ① 1 (U+0031) The circle disappears

NFKC is not a universally better NFC. A sentence explaining “the difference between ① and 1” can become one explaining “the difference between 1 and 1.” Compatibility distinctions can carry meaning in mathematical and technical material, so merging them indiscriminately is inappropriate. Unicode normalization standard, UAX #15

NFC does not preserve the original bytes either: the first row changes both the code-point count and the UTF-8 bytes. Calling our policy conservative describes its narrower range of equivalences; it is not a promise of losslessness for every application. We retain original_text and separately produce the training text. This records what the model will receive and allows another policy to be applied to the original later.

Our training text undergoes exactly three transformations: remove one leading U+FEFF marker, convert CRLF and CR newlines to LF, and apply NFC. Removing the leading marker is itself a deliberate policy choice. A corpus studying file encodings might need to preserve it. The report records these choices instead of hiding them behind a vague label such as “standard cleaning.”

def normalize_text(text: str) -> str:
    text = text.removeprefix("\ufeff")
    text = text.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace("\r", "\n")
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)

docs.title: Ignore whitespace for a count without deleting it from training text
docs.text:
str.strip() returns a string with leading and trailing whitespace removed, including spaces and tabs as well as newlines. Python str.strip

text = "    return x + 1\n"
count_view = text.strip()    # "return x + 1"，只用于计数
training_text = text        # 仍包含四个行首空格和末尾换行

Writing text.strip() back to the training record loses the first code line's indentation. Stripping every line and joining the results loses the indentation hierarchy throughout the block. Even when a fragment cannot run independently, cleaning should not silently change its structure in the original context.

The program therefore creates views for separate purposes. Training text retains its whitespace. Length measurement temporarily ignores whitespace at the two ends of the whole text. Repeated-line measurement additionally ignores whitespace at both ends of each line and omits empty lines. Neither measurement view replaces text. Two differently indented lines may therefore compare as equal in the diagnostic view while retaining their original indentation in saved code.

Figure 6.1　Follow the text path to see what is saved, then the measurement branch to see where decisions come from. Measurements never replace the training text. Each record has one final outcome, while diagnostic hits can overlap: thirteen records and ten hits use different counting units. Numbers come from this chapter's teaching fixture.

Open SVG PNG · 2× Vector PDF Scroll on narrow screens; open the image for full size.

docs.title: Make the rules concrete with 13 records
docs.text:
The input is examples/book/fixtures/cleaning_records.jsonl; open it in an editor to inspect every line. The first record has the following structure. Subsequent records use the same fields and deliberately include some invalid cases.

{"id":"c01","source":"web","language":"en","kind":"prose","text":"Café by the sea."}

id locates a sample; source names its source group; language is a label supplied by the input; kind distinguishes ordinary text, prose, from code; and text holds the content. No language-identification model runs here, so the language label is not a prediction made by this program. The first four fields must be nonempty strings, text must be a string, and kind must be one of the two supported values. These constraints on fields and types form a schema.

Structure is checked before text. text: 42 is a type error: silently converting it to "42" before judging its length would conceal the problem. Invalid JSON may not even define a complete object; we do not guess its ID from a partial line. These cases receive invalid_schema and invalid_json, respectively. The reader also rejects NaN, Infinity, and numbers outside its supported finite floating-point range, such as 1e999, recording them as invalid_json. The last case is a limit of this reader, not a claim that 1e999 violates JSON syntax; the rejection log preserves the original line. After schema validation, the program checks that the normalized text can be encoded as UTF-8. JSON escapes can represent lone surrogate code points that are not valid UTF-8 text; these receive invalid_unicode. The default fixture does not trigger this case, but the report retains its zero count.

Following the previous chapter's unambiguous-input policy, repeated names within any JSON object, including nested objects, also receive invalid_json. Otherwise {"text":42,"text":"A sufficiently long text"} silently becomes an object containing only the last text, hiding the first value from schema validation. The rejection log preserves the original line for repair rather than guessing which value the source intended.

Valid text is evaluated with the following settings. Length means the number of code points in the normalized text after temporarily excluding leading and trailing whitespace.

Rule Decision in this run Reason for the choice Empty text Reject an empty measurement view Spaces, tabs, and newlines alone provide no content for this example Minimum length At least 12 for prose, at least 1 for code Demonstrate different domain policies; 12 is not a universal quality boundary Maximum length Reject above 120 Demonstrate a processing limit with a small fixture; this does not declare long documents poor quality Repeated lines For prose only: at least 3 nonempty lines and duplicate fraction at least 0.6 Demonstrate repeated navigation; repeated code statements may be legitimate

We also need an unambiguous duplicate fraction. Let \(n_{\mathrm{line}}\) be the number of nonempty comparison lines and \(u_{\mathrm{line}}\) the number of distinct line contents. Define:

\[ ho_{\mathrm{line}}= egin{cases} 1-\dfrac{u_{\mathrm{line}}}{n_{\mathrm{line}}}, & n_{\mathrm{line}}>0,\ 0, & n_{\mathrm{line}}=0. \end{cases} \]

Keeping one copy of every distinct line would leave \(u_{\mathrm{line}}\) lines. The excess copies therefore number \(n_{\mathrm{line}}-u_{\mathrm{line}}\). For three copies of “首页,” the counts are 3 and 1, so \( ho_{\mathrm{line}}=2/3\), above 0.6. Three different lines give zero. This measure compares complete lines within one document; it is not a measure of similarity between documents, which we introduce in the next chapter.

The table gives hand-derived expectations for the default rules. denotes a newline. “121 a's” abbreviates the display; the fixture contains all 121 letters.

Line / ID Text or problem Primary outcome All diagnostic hits 1 / c01 Café by the sea.; 16 code points after NFC kept None 2 / c02 return x + 1 ; code kept None 3 / c03 Ａ＋①＝２，这些字形先保留。; 14 code points kept None 4 / c04 ; whitespace only empty empty, too_short 5 / c05 短定义。; 4 code points too_short too_short 6 / c06 首页 首页 首页; 8 code points too_short too_short, repeated_line 7 / c07 121 copies of a too_long too_long 8 / c08 Three lines of 重复的导航行; 20 code points repeated_line repeated_line 9 / c09 text is the number 42 invalid_schema invalid_schema 10 / no parseable ID JSON truncated after "text": invalid_json invalid_json 11 / c11 Unsupported kind value table invalid_schema invalid_schema 12 / c12 A short note about rain. kept None 13 / c13 Three indented pass lines; code kept None

Two details deserve a close look. The length of c06 is \(2+1+2+1+2=8\): surrounding whitespace is excluded, but each of the two internal newlines still contributes one code point. The duplicate fraction of c13 is also \(2/3\), but its kind is code, so the repeated-line rule does not apply. A high measured value can therefore coexist with an empty diagnostics list. A measurement and a rejection decision are different objects.

c05, whose text means “short definition,” exposes a limitation of the rule. A short definition does not become worthless merely because it has four code points. We intentionally retain this counterexample. Understanding a cleaning policy means being able to explain why c06 is rejected and to identify why rejecting c05 might conflict with the intended corpus.

docs.title: Why keep both a primary reason and every hit?
docs.text:
A whitespace-only text is both empty and shorter than 12. c06 is both short and repetitive. Incrementing “documents removed” for every rule hit would count both records twice, producing numbers that no longer correspond to the files.

The program stores one primary_reason per input and a potentially multi-valued diagnostics list. The order is fixed: invalid JSON, invalid schema, invalid text Unicode, empty text, too short, too long, repeated lines. The first hit supplies the primary reason; no hit means kept. When parsing or schema validation fails, later text measurements are undefined, so the program does not invent them. For valid text, it evaluates every applicable text rule and retains all its hits.

Let \(n_{\mathrm{input}}\) be the number of nonblank input lines, \(n_{\mathrm{kept}}\) the number retained, and \(n_{\mathrm{rejected},r}\) the number whose primary rejection reason is rule \(r\). Every input belongs to exactly one category. Partitioning the inputs into those categories and adding their sizes gives:

\[ n_{\mathrm{input}} =n_{\mathrm{kept}}+\sum_r n_{\mathrm{rejected},r}. \]

For the default fixture:

\[ 13=5+\underbrace{(1+2+0+1+2+1+1)}_{8\text{ rejected records}}. \]

The terms inside the parentheses follow the rule order above. This equation conserves input records. It does not conserve bytes, code points, or tokens. If documents are divided into smaller segments, record the parent-to-segment relationship separately; input documents and output segments cannot be substituted into the same count equation.

All-hit counts answer a different question: how many inputs triggered rule \(r\)? Here too_short has three hits and repeated_line has two, while their primary counts are two and one. All rule hits total 10, exceeding the eight rejected records because of overlap. The report therefore separates primary_counts from diagnostic_counts.

It also gives a stage table obtained by subtracting primary rejections in rule order. This is an accounting view; it does not mean diagnostics stop being evaluated after the first rejection.

Completed check Primary rejections at this stage Remaining records Nonblank input lines 0 13 invalid_json 1 12 invalid_schema 2 10 invalid_unicode 0 10 empty 1 9 too_short 2 7 too_long 1 6 repeated_line 1 5

The minimum-length stage removes two records: \(2/9\approx22.2\%\) of the nine entering that stage, or \(2/13\approx15.4\%\) of all inputs. Either fraction can be useful, but its denominator must be stated. Reordering rules can also change the primary-reason distribution even when it leaves the retained set unchanged.

docs.title: Run the program and inspect its files
docs.text:
The program is examples/book/cleaning_walkthrough.py and uses only the Python standard library. Run the following from the repository root. If .venv was created following the environment chapter, use that same interpreter. For this project's verification work, CPU execution takes place on the designated remote host; editing the chapter does not require running it locally.

.venv/bin/python examples/book/cleaning_walkthrough.py \
  --output outputs/book-cleaning-v1

--input defaults to the bundled fixture, so no download or missing input path is required. Existing output directories are rejected; give a new directory name for another run. The default terminal summary should contain input_records: 13, kept_records: 5, and rejected_records: 8. These numbers first come from the reasoning above. After execution, use the files from that run as evidence rather than presenting the hand-derived table as an execution log.

The output directory contains three files, each answering a separate question:

File Actual contents What to inspect kept.jsonl Five retained records; original_text stores input text, text stores normalized text, and cleaning stores the rule version and input line Accent composition in c01, indentation in c02, fullwidth characters and the circled number in c03 rejected.jsonl Primary reason, diagnostics, original object, and input line for each rejection; text metrics when defined Overlapping hits for c04 and c06, and the parse error on line 10 report.json Parameters, counts, grouped statistics, per-record decisions, Unicode examples, and version identifiers Compare each result with the tables above

Output JSON represents non-ASCII characters using \uXXXX escapes, so an editor may show escapes instead of visible Chinese text. Parsing the JSON restores the same Unicode strings; this does not delete Chinese content. The representation also lets the rejection log preserve lone surrogate code points that cannot themselves be encoded as UTF-8 text.

The next command reads the actual outputs and prints the details we want to inspect. It does not rerun cleaning or modify files.

.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path

root = Path("outputs/book-cleaning-v1")
report = json.loads((root / "report.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
rows = [json.loads(line) for line in (root / "kept.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()]
print("Primary outcomes:", report["primary_counts"])
print("All hits:", report["diagnostic_counts"])
print("Retained IDs:", [row["id"] for row in rows])
for row in rows:
    if row["id"] in {"c01", "c02", "c03"}:
        print(row["id"], repr(row["original_text"]), "->", repr(row["text"]))
PY

repr displays newlines as \n and surrounds a string with quotes, making leading spaces easier to inspect. Retained IDs should be c01, c02, c03, c12, c13 in input order. The text of c02 should still start with four spaces.

Several report fields need precise interpretations:

Report field Exact meaning input_sha256, script_sha256 SHA-256 digests of the input bytes and current script bytes, identifying the input and implementation python_version, unicode_version The running interpreter version and the Unicode database version used by unicodedata parameters, rule_order Thresholds, normalization choices, rule applicability, and primary-reason priority input_records, ignored_blank_lines Nonblank input lines and skipped blank lines; an ordinary final newline does not create an extra line primary_counts, diagnostic_counts, stages Exclusive outcomes, potentially overlapping rule hits, and stage counts after primary rejections groups, group_scope Counts grouped by supplied source/language/kind for schema-valid records only; invalid JSON and invalid schema are excluded decisions Input line, ID when available, primary outcome, and diagnostics; valid text additionally has lengths, line counts, duplicate fraction, and related metrics unicode_examples Original, NFC, and NFKC strings, code points, and UTF-8 bytes for the three examples count_conservation The program checked conservation of primary counts; it does not certify corpus quality

Ten fixture records pass the schema, so the input counts in groups sum to 10 while global input_records is 13. The difference follows from the stated scope. The other three records should not be forced into a guessed language group. Counting records with invalid provenance separately is usually more interpretable than inventing labels for them.

Threshold decisions must preserve the mathematical boundary: “at least 0.2” includes exactly \(1/5\). With five lines and four distinct contents, the program compares the standard-library value Fraction(1, 5) with the threshold, avoiding rounding in 1 - 4 / 5. The parameter is first parsed as a Python float, then interpreted as the decimal number printed by its str; that representation is recorded. duplicate_comparison_lines counts the excess copies, while the approximate duplicate_line_fraction is for display, not the final decision. See floating-point representation and rounding.

Including equality also defines the endpoints. A threshold of zero rejects every eligible prose record with at least three nonempty lines, even without repetition. At one, this rule rejects none: finitely many nonempty lines always have a duplicate fraction below one. These endpoints check implementation behavior, rather than recommend cleaning settings. The rule version is now cleaning-walkthrough-v2.

A UTF-8 decoding failure aborts the whole input. A single JSON or schema failure instead enters the rejection log while other records continue. The program finishes its analysis before creating the output directory and writes the report last. An interrupted disk write can still leave a partial directory. Without all three complete files and a readable report, the run is not a successful result.

docs.title: Change one threshold and see what comes back
docs.text:
Keep the input fixed and lower only the prose minimum length from 12 to 4:

.venv/bin/python examples/book/cleaning_walkthrough.py \
  --output outputs/book-cleaning-min4 \
  --min-prose-chars 4

Predict before inspecting the output. c05 is exactly four code points long and now passes. c06 is no longer too short but still has repeated lines, so it remains rejected with repeated_line as its primary reason. The expected retained count rises from five to six, while rejections fall from eight to seven. The primary too_short count becomes zero and the primary repeated_line count becomes two. Whitespace-only c04 still triggers both empty and too_short. A rule change can therefore alter either the retained set or only the attribution for an already rejected record.

This does not prove that the new rule is better. It only shows that one short text returned. Whether it belongs in the corpus depends on the intended material and on further samples. If most short records are navigation, buttons, or extraction fragments, lowering the threshold may also bring back substantial noise.

Language and domain affect this tradeoff. Equal Chinese and English code-point counts do not guarantee equal information content. Short code lines, mathematical symbols, and repeated lines of poetry can all be legitimate. Real policies may use separate thresholds by source, language, and content type, but such choices should follow stratified inspection rather than unexamined exceptions. This program implements only separate prose/code minimum lengths and grouped reporting. It does not automatically choose language-specific thresholds or classify the quality of poetry and mathematics.

Stratified inspection means dividing samples into meaningful groups and examining each group. Our code group retains 2/2 records, while the Chinese short-definition source retains 0/1. A global 5/13 cannot describe both differences. Groups containing one or two examples do not estimate production false-rejection rates, however; they show whether the report can locate a problem.

Estimating false rejection requires additional labels saying “should retain for this training objective” or “should reject.” Within the same labeled sample, define:

\[ \text{false rejection rate} =\frac{\text{records that should be retained but were rejected}} {\text{all records that should be retained}}. \]

This fraction requires at least one record that should be retained. With a zero denominator, report it as undefined rather than zero. The denominator includes correctly retained useful records, so sampling only rejected records cannot estimate this fraction. If two of ten human-confirmed useful records are rejected, the false-rejection rate is 20%. That is a different question from what fraction of all rejected records were rejected incorrectly. Oversampling threshold-adjacent examples is useful for finding problems, but the resulting fraction describes that boundary sample and cannot be directly extrapolated to the corpus. The program does not automatically supply human quality labels, and its keep_rate is not the false-rejection rate above.

docs.title: From this example to a larger corpus
docs.text:
The program holds its small input and decisions in memory so that records, outputs, and report entries can be followed one by one. Production corpora need chunked input processing, recovery after interruption, stable record identities, and a stronger provenance schema. Web sources additionally need article extraction, and quality decisions may need evaluated classifiers. A successful run of this example does not establish those capabilities.

The retained text is now a specified version of the text view. The next chapter compares documents on a fixed view and explains why “the same meaning,” “the same string,” and “the same training example” are different notions. Tokenization and training-window construction follow afterward. Each stage then answers its own question: here we checked how text changed and why records were retained or rejected, instead of treating a successful token-encoding command as evidence that cleaning worked.

docs.title: 7　Deduplication: controlling how often the same information appears
Why cleaning is not enough
docs.text:
The previous chapter asked whether a record is worth keeping. A good article republished a hundred times may pass every cleaning rule a hundred times. Training on those copies does not provide a hundred independent pieces of knowledge: it repeatedly emphasizes the same content. Photocopying a page a hundred times makes a book thicker without adding a hundred pages of new knowledge.

Duplication first changes the training distribution. Consider an equal-length document collection containing just two kinds of content: nine copies of one article and one copy of another. Uniform document sampling selects the first content with probability \(9/10\) and the second with probability \(1/10\). Keeping one copy of each changes both probabilities to \(1/2\). The sampler did not change, but copy counts acted as implicit sampling weights. If lengths differ, or sampling operates on tokens or training windows, probabilities must be calculated under that protocol instead.

Copies can also cross an evaluation boundary. If training contains an article and validation contains its mirror, validation may test predictions of previously encountered passages. The original study by Lee et al. examines training duplication, memorization, and training–evaluation overlap. It motivates checking these issues; its reported benefits are not measurements of this project.

Deduplication involves three questions: what counts as the same content, how to find potentially matching documents in a large collection, and which document to retain. These correspond to the comparison representation, candidate retrieval, and retention policy. We will connect them using five short original documents. The small tables are constructed teaching examples; the accompanying script turns their calculations into inspectable artifacts.

docs.title: Define what is compared before computing a digest
docs.text:
These are all five texts in examples/book/dedup_documents.jsonl. The JSON escape \n represents an LF newline, while \r\n represents CRLF. Decoding them produces one or two control characters respectively. The color words are convenient labels for calculation, without additional semantic significance.

Document ID Source JSON representation of text Name after exact deduplication d01 notes "red blue green amber\n" Document A d02 mirror "red blue green amber\r\n" A's copy d03 notes "red blue green amber gold\n" Document B d04 notes "blue green amber gold\n" Document C d05 notes "red blue green violet silver\n" Document D

Their original bytes make d01 and d02 different. We first define this experiment's rule: normalize Unicode to NFC and replace CRLF with LF, preserving case, punctuation, indentation, trailing spaces, and other characters. NFC handles canonically equivalent representations, such as a precomposed “é” and an “e followed by a combining accent.” It neither translates text nor decides whether documents have the same meaning. Canonical equivalence can still collapse encoding distinctions between some symbols, so this is a chosen comparison representation, not proof of semantic losslessness. This rule does not replace every standalone CR either.

Call the resulting string the comparison text. It is used for matching, while the selected representative keeps its original text. This distinction matters: a similarity representation may be coarser than the training text, but it should not silently rewrite that text. Removing all spaces might simplify some webpage comparisons while destroying code indentation.

import hashlib
import unicodedata

def comparison_text(text):
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text).replace("\r\n", "\n")

def exact_key(text):
    compared = comparison_text(text)
    return hashlib.sha256(compared.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

SHA-256 maps a byte string of arbitrary length to a fixed-length digest, commonly displayed as 64 hexadecimal characters. Think of the digest as an index label: group documents with the same label, then compare their complete comparison texts. Identical inputs have identical digests. The converse is not a logical guarantee, because different inputs can have a hash collision. Our script compares full comparison texts after matching digests. Even a test that deliberately gives every document the same digest therefore does not merge all five records.

Representative selection also needs a rule. This experiment processes document IDs in lexicographic order and keeps the first ID for identical comparison texts. Thus d02 → d01, while d01, d03, d04, and d05 represent themselves. ID order determines the result, so reversing input lines does not change it. A production project might prefer a source with more complete permission metadata or a more complete article, but must record priorities and tie-breaking.

This is exact deduplication. “Exact” refers to equality of the explicitly defined comparison texts, not byte-for-byte equality of the original files. A copy's provenance should not disappear with its text: representative mappings provide a way to trace copies, while the actual corpus catalog must also retain their source and permission records.

docs.title: Turn text into a comparable set
docs.text:
Exact deduplication leaves A, B, C, and D. B differs from A by just one word, but their full-text digests already differ. Recognizing this overlap requires a different comparison representation.

We split on whitespace and take adjacent pairs of words, called word bigram shingles. Splitting A gives:

red | blue | green | amber

A window of width 2 moves one word at a time, producing three fragments:

(red, blue)    (blue, green)    (green, amber)

This splitting rule is for deduplication; it is not the language model's tokenizer. The model tokenizer's vocabulary and token IDs are introduced later. Whitespace splitting should not be assumed appropriate for Chinese, other languages without word spaces, or code. Character fragments or domain-specific segmentation may be preferable, with the chosen rule version recorded.

To make the tables readable, label the six distinct fragments as follows. These letters name set elements in this example; they are not model parameters or tokenizer IDs.

Label Word bigram a (red, blue) b (blue, green) c (green, amber) d (amber, gold) e (green, violet) f (violet, silver)

Let \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B,\mathcal C,\mathcal D\) denote the shingle sets of documents A, B, C, and D:

\[ \mathcal A=\{a,b,c\},\qquad \mathcal B=\{a,b,c,d\},\qquad \mathcal C=\{b,c,d\},\qquad \mathcal D=\{a,b,e,f\}. \]

A set records each distinct fragment once, without order or frequency. The text red blue red blue has fragments at three positions, but its set contains only (red, blue) and (blue, red). This representation preserves some local word order while losing document structure and fragment counts. It helps find overlap, but does not understand meaning or independently measure repetition within a document.

Jaccard similarity measures set overlap. For finite sets \(\mathcal S,\mathcal T\) whose union is nonempty, define:

\[ J(\mathcal S,\mathcal T) =\frac{|\mathcal S\cap\mathcal T|}{|\mathcal S\cup\mathcal T|}. \]

The intersection symbol \(\cap\) means elements present in both sets; the union symbol \(\cup\) means elements present in either set. Vertical bars count distinct elements. The numerator counts shared kinds of fragment, and the denominator counts all kinds involved, giving a value between 0 and 1.

A and B share \(a,b,c\), and together contain \(a,b,c,d\). Therefore:

\[ \mathcal A\cap\mathcal B=\{a,b,c\},\qquad \mathcal A\cup\mathcal B=\{a,b,c,d\},\qquad J(\mathcal A,\mathcal B)=\frac34. \]

A and D both contain \(a,b\), but their union is \(a,b,c,e,f\). Thus \(J(\mathcal A,\mathcal D)=2/5\); having two shared fragments alone does not establish duplication. The complete hand calculation is:

Document pair Intersection size Union size Jaccard A, B 3 4 \(3/4\) A, C 2 4 \(1/2\) A, D 2 5 \(2/5\) B, C 3 4 \(3/4\) B, D 2 6 \(1/3\) C, D 1 6 \(1/6\)

A one-word document has no word bigrams. Comparing two empty sets gives \(0/0\), and MinHash also has no minimum element to select. The teaching script rejects such input. A real pipeline must route short documents separately or define an appropriate alternative; assigning all empty sets a shared signature and merging them is not a sound default.

docs.title: MinHash: compress a large set into a short signature
docs.text:
Four documents have only six pairs, so calculating every Jaccard value is easy. But \(N\) documents have \(N(N-1)/2\) unordered pairs: each document has \(N-1\) partners, and that counts each pair twice. Even fast set comparisons become expensive as document counts grow.

MinHash first computes a short signature for each document. Think of it as several representative elements selected by a common rule. The goal is to make similar sets more likely to agree at the same signature position. These short signatures can then organize candidate retrieval.

Start with one signature position. Order the complete universe \(\{a,b,c,d,e,f\}\), and let every document search the same order for its first element. For example:

\[ d\prec c\prec b\prec a\prec e\prec f. \]

The symbol \(\prec\) means “earlier in this order.” A lacks \(d\), so its first available element is \(c\). B and C contain \(d\), so both choose \(d\). D lacks \(d,c\), so it chooses \(b\). This round gives signature values \(c,d,d,b\).

Let \(\pi\) denote a permutation and \(\operatorname{rank}_\pi(u)\) the position of element \(u\) in it. The selection can be written as:

\[ h_\pi(\mathcal S) =\underset{u\in\mathcal S}{\operatorname{argmin}}\, \operatorname{rank}_\pi(u). \]

Here \(\operatorname{argmin}\) returns the element with the smallest position, rather than that position's numerical value. Textbooks and libraries may instead store its permutation rank or hash value. With a collision-free permutation, checking equality within the same round is equivalent. We store element labels to make the example inspectable. Documents must not use unrelated permutations independently: that would break the comparison intended here.

For hand calculation, explicitly choose four orders. These are fixed illustrative permutations, not a claimed independent uniform random sample.

Signature row Order from first to last A B C D 1 a b c d e f a a b a 2 b c d a e f b b b b 3 d c b a e f c d d b 4 c d a b e f c c c a

A's signature is \((a,b,c,c)\), B's is \((a,b,d,c)\), C's is \((b,b,d,c)\), and D's is \((a,b,b,a)\). An element can occur repeatedly within a column because rows use different permutations. A column is not a sample of four distinct document elements drawn without replacement.

docs.title: Why collision probability equals Jaccard similarity
docs.text:
The following property concerns a randomized construction, not a probability claim about the four fixed orders above. Let \(\mathcal S,\mathcal T\) be nonempty finite sets. Choose one permutation uniformly from all permutations of a shared finite universe. Write \(\mathcal U=\mathcal S\cup\mathcal T\), and examine its earliest element, \(u_\star\).

First, each element of \(\mathcal U\) has the same chance to be earliest. A uniform random permutation favors no element: exchanging two element names pairs every ordering in which one is earliest with an ordering in which the other is earliest. The possible earliest elements are mutually exclusive and cover all cases, so each has probability \(1/|\mathcal U|\).

Next, consider two cases:

  1. If \(u_\star\in\mathcal S\cap\mathcal T\), both sets contain it, and no element of their union is earlier. Both therefore select it, giving equal signatures.
  2. If \(u_\star\) belongs to only one set, that set selects it and the other cannot. Their signatures differ.

Thus signatures agree if and only if the union's earliest element belongs to the intersection. Add the probabilities for each intersection element being earliest:

\[ \begin{aligned} \Pr\!\left[h_\pi(\mathcal S)=h_\pi(\mathcal T)\right] &=\Pr\!\left[u_\star\in\mathcal S\cap\mathcal T\right]\\ &=\sum_{u\in\mathcal S\cap\mathcal T}\frac1{|\mathcal S\cup\mathcal T|}\\ &=\frac{|\mathcal S\cap\mathcal T|}{|\mathcal S\cup\mathcal T|}\\ &=J(\mathcal S,\mathcal T). \end{aligned} \]

For A and B, the union has four elements. An earliest element of \(a,b,c\) gives a collision, while \(d\) does not. The collision probability is therefore \(3/4\). This describes repeated random choices of permutations. It does not mean that after observing one matching signature, the documents have a \(3/4\) probability of being duplicates. That different claim requires a definition of true duplication and a model of the document population.

Real text has a huge shingle universe, so implementations do not explicitly generate a full random permutation of every possible element. They commonly use seeded hash families to assign an order and retain a minimum value. How well the family approximates equal chances of being minimal, and how it handles collisions, depend on the implementation. Different integer seeds alone do not prove independent uniform permutations. Charikar's original research account distinguishes exact min-wise independence from approximate properties. Engineering reports should record the hash algorithm, seeds, and version.

If we independently sample \(m_{\mathrm{hash}}\) ideal permutations, let \(I_j\) be 1 when row \(j\) agrees and 0 otherwise. The proportion of matching rows is:

\[ \widehat q=\frac1{m_{\mathrm{hash}}}\sum_{j=1}^{m_{\mathrm{hash}}}I_j. \]

Write the true Jaccard value as \(q=J(\mathcal S,\mathcal T)\). Each \(I_j\) equals 1 with probability \(q\) and 0 with probability \(1-q\). Its average, or expectation, is therefore \(1\cdot q+0\cdot(1-q)=q\). Expectation is linear over sums, so \(\mathbb E[\widehat q]=(m_{\mathrm{hash}}q)/m_{\mathrm{hash}}=q\). This is unbiasedness: the long-run average over repeated random constructions equals the target, not every individual estimate.

Variance is the expected squared deviation from the mean. For a variable with only two possible values, calculate it directly from those cases:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(I_j) =q(1-q)^2+(1-q)(0-q)^2 =q(1-q). \]

The first term is for value 1 and the second for value 0, each weighted by its probability. Under independent rows, variances add; dividing the sum by \(m_{\mathrm{hash}}^2\) yields:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\widehat q)= \frac{q(1-q)}{m_{\mathrm{hash}}}. \]

More rows can therefore reduce estimation variability while requiring more storage. In our four fixed rows, A and B happen to agree in \(3/4\) of positions, as do B and C. But A and D agree in \(2/4\), differing from their true \(2/5\). This fixed small table is not a measurement of a randomized estimator's accuracy.

docs.title: LSH: match a whole band to enter the candidate list
docs.text:
Short signatures reduce individual comparison cost, but comparing every document pair still takes quadratically many comparisons. Locality-sensitive hashing, or LSH, groups signatures into buckets so that similar documents are more likely to share a bucket. A bucket is simply a labeled collection of documents; sharing one makes documents eligible for pairwise verification.

Split our four signature rows into two bands, each containing two consecutive rows. Compare only within the same band. Two documents become candidates if all their rows in that band match; a match in any one band is enough. Thus matching all rows within a band is an AND condition, while matching at least one band is an OR condition.

Document Band 1: rows 1 and 2 Band 2: rows 3 and 4 A (a,b) (c,c) B (a,b) (d,c) C (b,b) (d,c) D (a,b) (b,a)

Band 1 places A, B, and D in one bucket, generating pairs A—B, A—D, and B—D. Band 2 groups B and C, adding B—C. Deduplicating the pair list gives four candidates. A pair found in both bands still needs verification only once. Bucket keys must include the band index: a value from band 1 must not match a value from band 2 merely because their tuples happen to be equal.

Figure 7.1　Start with the signature bands and their four candidate pairs, then compare the exact Jaccard values on solid and dashed edges. Follow retention order last: once B is represented by A, B cannot justify removing C. Four candidates, two threshold edges, and one near-duplicate removal are different quantities.

Open SVG PNG · 2× Vector PDF Scroll on narrow screens; open the image for full size.

docs.title: Deriving the candidate probability
docs.text:
Let the true Jaccard similarity be \(q\). Each band contains \(r_{\mathrm{LSH}}\) rows, there are \(b_{\mathrm{LSH}}\) bands, and the total row count is \(m_{\mathrm{hash}}=b_{\mathrm{LSH}}r_{\mathrm{LSH}}\). Assume that rows come from independent uniform random permutations.

  • One row matches with probability \(q\).
  • Every row of a specified band matches with probability \(q^{r_{\mathrm{LSH}}}\), because probabilities multiply for independent events occurring together.
  • That band fails to match completely with probability \(1-q^{r_{\mathrm{LSH}}}\).
  • Every band fails to match completely with probability \((1-q^{r_{\mathrm{LSH}}})^{b_{\mathrm{LSH}}}\), since bands use disjoint groups of independent rows.
  • Matching at least one band is the complement of the last event, giving:
\[ P_{\mathrm{candidate}}(q) =1-\left(1-q^{r_{\mathrm{LSH}}}\right)^{b_{\mathrm{LSH}}}. \]

This is the banding formula often written \(1-(1-s^r)^b\). We use subscripted band parameters and \(q\) for similarity to distinguish them from the book's batch and token-stream notation. The AND–OR construction and formula can also be checked against the Stanford CS336 deduplication lecture source.

In the ideal randomized setting with two rows per band and two bands, a pair with similarity \(q=3/4\) becomes a candidate with probability:

\[ 1-\left(1-\left(\frac34\right)^2\right)^2 =1-\left(\frac7{16}\right)^2 =\frac{207}{256} \approx 0.8086. \]

It still has probability \(49/256\) of being missed. A pair with similarity only \(q=2/5\) has a nonzero candidate probability too:

\[ 1-\left(1-\left(\frac25\right)^2\right)^2 =1-\left(\frac{21}{25}\right)^2 =\frac{184}{625} =0.2944. \]

These are theoretical probabilities under the randomized model. Our four fixed orders produce one deterministic candidate list; they do not establish a measured recall of 80.86%. LSH can miss similar documents and retrieve dissimilar ones. It does not implement a perfect hard threshold.

Holding rows per band fixed, more bands increase the chance of at least one match and can increase verification cost. Holding the number of bands fixed, more rows per band make a full band match harder. With a fixed total signature length, the two parameters are also constrained by their product. Choose them using candidate volume, misses, and false matches on actual data, rather than treating a single “deduplication threshold” as the whole specification.

docs.title: Candidates, similar pairs, and deletion decisions differ
docs.text:
Choose a final similarity threshold of \(q_\star=3/4\) for this teaching experiment. This value exposes the decision process; it is not a production default for every corpus. Read the complete shingle sets again and compute exact Jaccard values for the four candidates:

Candidate pair Exact Jaccard Meets \(q_\star\)? A—B \(3/4\) Yes A—D \(2/5\) No B—C \(3/4\) Yes B—D \(1/3\) No

Deleting immediately after a bucket match could wrongly remove D because it shares band 1 with A. Verification rejects that candidate, but verification still does not establish factual equivalence. It precisely applies the current set-similarity rule. A changed date, negation, or program operator may be an important difference worth preserving.

A subtler problem concerns A, B, and C:

\[ J(\mathcal A,\mathcal B)=\frac34,\qquad J(\mathcal B,\mathcal C)=\frac34,\qquad J(\mathcal A,\mathcal C)=\frac12. \]

A meeting the threshold with B, and B meeting it with C, does not imply that A meets it with C. In mathematical language, thresholded similarity is not transitive. Exact string equality is different: if A equals B and B equals C, A must equal C.

Draw each document as a point and each above-threshold pair as an edge. A—B—C forms a path. A connected component is a group of points reachable from each other through paths of edges, so all three belong to the same component. Keeping only the smallest-ID document A in that component would remove B and C, even though A and C do not meet the threshold. This chain merge follows from the clustering policy, rather than an error in Jaccard calculation.

Our script uses a stricter deletion rule. Process IDs in ascending order; remove the current document only if it is a direct candidate of an already-retained representative and its exact Jaccard meets the threshold. If several retained representatives qualify, choose the one with the smallest ID. The resulting steps are:

  1. A comes first and has no earlier representative, so keep A.
  2. B is a direct candidate of retained A with similarity \(3/4\). Remove B and record d03 → d01.
  3. C is similar to B, but B was removed. C has no qualifying candidate edge to retained A, so keep C.
  4. D is a candidate of retained A but has similarity only \(2/5\). D and C are not candidates, so keep D.

This avoids the example's chain merge. It does not guarantee that the retained collection has no genuinely similar pairs, since candidate retrieval can still miss them. It is not a globally optimal representative selection either: the outcome depends on the explicit ID priority. Production decisions must consider permissions, quality, completeness, and language coverage rather than treating smallest ID as a universal quality measure.

Deletion and splitting policies can also differ. To prevent evaluation overlap, the connected component A, B, C can be required to stay in one dataset partition while retaining both A and C within it. The first policy conservatively protects the evaluation boundary; the second limits deletion. Record these groups separately so that “assign together” does not silently become “keep only one.”

docs.title: Run these documents instead of only describing the algorithm
docs.text:
The executable entry point is examples/book/dedup_walkthrough.py. It uses the Python 3.10+ standard library, without JAX, a GPU, downloads, or extra dependencies. collections, fractions, hashlib, and itertools are standard-library modules. The script handles the supplied six-shingle teaching fixture; it is not a production deduplicator accepting arbitrary webpage corpora.

On a CPU machine with the repository cloned, run from the repository root. Project maintenance runs these commands on the designated remote CPU node:

python3 examples/book/dedup_checks.py
python3 examples/book/dedup_walkthrough.py --output outputs/book-dedup-v1

The output directory must not already exist. Use a new name, such as outputs/book-dedup-v2, for another comparison so previous evidence remains intact. The script reads the adjacent dedup_documents.jsonl automatically and produces:

Artifact or report field What to inspect report.json: exact_keys and exact_representatives Check that d01 and d02 share a key, and that d02 maps to d01 shingle_sets, illustrative_permutations, signatures Match actual arrays to the set and permutation tables band_buckets, candidate_pair_reviews Inspect band members, the four distinct candidate pairs, their intersections, unions, and exact similarities representative_decisions, final_representatives Distinguish a qualifying pair from the representative ultimately selected for a document exhaustive_permutation_checks Enumerate all \(6!=720\) orders for each of six document pairs and compare collision fractions with exact Jaccard counts Separate document outcomes from pair-review activity deduped.jsonl Retained original records, including their original text and source

Here \(6!=6\times5\times4\times3\times2\times1=720\): six choices for the first position, five for the second, and so on. For A and B, hand calculation predicts 540 collisions out of 720 permutations because three of the four union elements belong to the intersection. Exhaustive enumeration checks this tiny example. It is neither a production algorithm for large corpora nor a replacement for the general proof.

The rules above imply these expected values:

{
  "input_documents": 5,
  "kept_documents": 3,
  "exact_removed_documents": 1,
  "near_removed_documents": 1,
  "candidate_pairs_reviewed": 4,
  "pairs_at_or_above_threshold": 2
}

This JSON is derived from the example; it is not presented as an execution log. Read your own generated report.json after running the script. Retained IDs should be d01,d04,d05; exact deduplication removes d02, and near-duplicate selection removes d03. The report also records the rule version, Python version, input-file SHA-256, and script SHA-256 so the materials used can be identified.

Document outcomes obey a conservation relationship:

\[ N_{\mathrm{input}} =N_{\mathrm{kept}} +N_{\mathrm{exact\ removed}} +N_{\mathrm{near\ removed}}, \qquad 5=3+1+1. \]

The three outcomes are disjoint and cover every input document. By contrast, candidate_pairs_reviewed=4 counts document pairs reviewed, and pairs_at_or_above_threshold=2 counts qualifying document pairs. Neither counts removed documents, and neither belongs on the right side of that equation. B participates in both qualifying edges A—B and B—C but remains just one document. Only B is removed: the number of edges and the number of removed points are different quantities.

The checks deliberately force digest collisions, reverse input order, and verify that empty sets and invalid band lengths are rejected. They target behaviors that can actually go wrong. If a result differs, find the first disagreeing intermediate table: for exact representatives, inspect normalization and IDs; for sets, inspect splitting and shingle width; for candidates, inspect permutations and bands; for retention, inspect representative selection. Do not merely adjust final counts to make them match.

docs.title: Put the teaching algorithm back into a data pipeline
docs.text:
The example exposes each decision but does not solve all large-corpus engineering problems. Reading JSONL through the current training-data entry point does not automatically run this chapter's MinHash/LSH process. The chapter script independently writes deduped.jsonl. Production deduplication should be an explicit, versioned upstream stage producing text, original-to-representative mappings, and candidate and decision reports, which can then be associated with tokenizer outputs and token manifests.

First define the scope. A source with no internal duplicates can still overlap other sources after a merge. Inspect within-source, cross-source, and training–validation overlap separately. Keeping shared copies under a single source can change language, domain, or licensed-source coverage. Reports should compare these distributions before and after deduplication rather than reporting only a removal percentage.

Next define the unit. This chapter compares whole documents. Long documents may share one paragraph while having low overall Jaccard similarity. Paragraph deduplication or repeated-substring detection can address that case, but removing an internal paragraph can break references, derivations, or code context. These operations need their own segmentation and retention rules; changing a document threshold does not implement them.

Then calibrate errors. Removing content that should have been retained is a false removal; missing documents that the intended policy considers duplicates is a miss. Inspect both retrieved candidates and nonretrieved pairs, or use a stronger independent retrieval method to search for omissions. Inspecting only candidates cannot estimate how much retrieval missed. Human judgments also need written criteria for factual updates, code changes, and permission variants.
