Finally account for resources and reproducibility. The script stores texts and sets in memory and enumerates permutations to explain probability. Real systems commonly need sharding, external sorting, or distributed indexes. A huge bucket full of webpage templates can still create many candidate pairs; LSH does not guarantee linear work on every dataset. Bucket limits, candidate truncation, or changed hash implementations can affect misses and must enter the rule version and report. A credible deduplicated corpus should explain not only how much was removed, but which documents were removed, why, and which representatives replaced them.

The next chapter addresses another boundary: once relationships between documents are known, how should training and validation sets be constructed so that validation better reflects prediction on unseen content?

docs.title: 8. Splits and contamination: define what “unseen” means
Better training performance does not necessarily mean better learning
docs.text:
A teacher assigns ten practice problems and uses the same ten problems in the next day's exam. A perfect score does not establish that the student understands the topic: memorizing the answers remains an explanation. Different questions testing the same knowledge provide better evidence for the ability we intended to measure.

Language model training has the same distinction. Training text participates in parameter updates, and reducing loss on repeatedly encountered data is the optimization objective. A validation set measures performance on data excluded from direct parameter updates and helps select configurations, training duration, and cleaning rules. A test set supplies the final evaluation after those choices are fixed; it should not repeatedly participate in them.

These names describe experimental roles, rather than three arbitrary folders. If we repeatedly inspect “test” scores to choose a model, that data has taken on the validation role. Selection has used its information even without backpropagation through it. “Unseen” therefore includes both exclusion from training updates and a clear limit on which development decisions may use the data.

Language models commonly compute loss by predicting the next token, and validation and testing can use the same objective. We first establish document membership; the next chapter explains tokenization in detail. The immediate question is which complete documents may enter training and which are reserved for evaluation.

docs.title: The evaluation question determines the split unit
docs.text:
“Randomly reserve one percent for validation” specifies a proportion without identifying what is sampled. Should chapters from the same book be sampled independently? Are ten websites mirroring an article ten independent objects? The answer depends on the claim we want to support.

Intended evaluation Objects to consider grouping Confound to prevent New documents from similar sources An original and its duplicate or near-duplicate versions Training already contains a mirror Unseen books Books Adjacent chapters appear in different sets New code projects Repositories or projects Files and branches from the same project cross sets Text from a future period Time boundaries and related document groups Training has used future information

This table is not an automatic policy. Temporal splits must still handle old articles republished later; project splits must consider copied code. Define the evaluation question, construct relevant groups, and only then choose proportions.

Deduplication from the previous chapter can supply useful relationships, but deciding which documents to retain and deciding which documents may cross sets are separate tasks. Complementary documents from one source can all be retained while sharing one split. Grouping can therefore be broader than the similarity conditions used to delete duplicates.

docs.title: Why independently splitting mirrors causes leakage
docs.text:
Suppose one article has \(m\) mirrors. Independently assign each record to validation with probability \(p\), and to training with probability \(1-p\). We consider only two sets here to make the probability argument explicit.

There are exactly two ways for the group to avoid crossing sets: all mirrors enter training, or all enter validation. Independence allows us to multiply probabilities, giving \((1-p)^m\) and \(p^m\). The events are mutually exclusive. Consequently,

\[ P(\text{duplicate group crosses train and validation}) =1-(1-p)^m-p^m. \]

For \(m=10\), the probability is approximately \(9.56\%\) when \(p=0.01\), and \(65.13\%\) when \(p=0.1\). Risk depends on group size and split proportion; it is not almost certain for every group regardless of the ratio. With many groups, even a modest individual risk deserves attention.

Group-level assignment makes one decision for the entire group and lets its records inherit the result. Provided the grouping is correct, that group's probability of crossing sets is zero. This does not establish that all mirrors were discovered: missing relationships can still cause leakage.

docs.title: Giving each group a stable assignment
docs.text:
The teaching fixture adds a split_group field to each record. Records d01 and d02 contain the same short text from two source types and both belong to guide-blue. Records d04 and d05 contain different project notes and both belong to project-cache. They illustrate duplicate relationships and shared-project relationships respectively.

We want two properties: changing file traversal order should not change existing assignments, and adding an unrelated group should not reshuffle all old data. One direct implementation hashes a stable group ID and maps the digest to a bucket. A bucket here is simply an integer from 0 to 9,999.

The core implementation is:

payload = json.dumps(
    ["book-group-split-v1", seed, group],
    ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":"),
).encode("utf-8")
bucket = int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(payload).digest()[:8], "big") % 10_000

The first step serializes the policy name, seed, and group ID. Field boundaries matter: plain concatenation would make "ab" + "c" indistinguishable from "a" + "bc". The second step computes SHA-256, takes its first eight bytes, and interprets them as a nonnegative big-endian integer. Big-endian means earlier bytes occupy more significant positions. Taking the remainder maps that integer to one of 10,000 buckets.

The seed is one input to this deterministic rule. Identical inputs always produce identical buckets; changing the seed defines another assignment. Python's built-in hash() is unsuitable as a direct persistent splitting rule because string and byte hashes use process-varying randomization by default. See Python's __hash__ documentation.

Buckets below 6,000 enter training, buckets from 6,000 through 7,999 enter validation, and the remainder enter testing. The 60% / 20% / 20% proportions are for demonstrating three sets with ten small groups, not a recommendation for production pretraining. Modulo reduction is not perfectly uniform because \(2^{64}\) is not divisible by 10,000. If the digest prefix is modeled as a uniform 64-bit value, bucket probabilities differ only minutely. Deterministic inputs establish stability; approximate proportions additionally depend on the groups and digest distribution. These are separate properties.

Stability also has limits. Group IDs derived from unstable file enumeration change when enumeration changes. A newly discovered relationship may require merging two old groups and reconsidering their membership. Stability under appending data means adding an independent group while preserving the rule and existing IDs, not immunity to arbitrary revisions of the grouping.

docs.title: Group proportions, document proportions, and token proportions differ
docs.text:
Approximately uniform assignment of groups does not give each set an exact document proportion. Let \(I_g\) indicate whether group \(g\) enters validation: it is one if the group enters and zero otherwise. Let \(w_g\) count its documents. Then the validation document count is

\[ N_{\mathrm{val}}=\sum_g w_g I_g. \]

In an idealized model, each group independently enters validation with probability \(p\). Since \(I_g\) equals one with probability \(p\), its mean is \(p\). Linearity of expectation gives

\[ \mathbb E[N_{\mathrm{val}}]=p\sum_g w_g. \]

This describes a long-run average, not an exact count in a particular split. To describe how outcomes fluctuate around that average, we use variance. For a random quantity \(Z\), define \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\mathbb E[(Z-\mathbb E[Z])^2]\): measure each outcome's distance from the mean, square it, and average. Squaring prevents positive and negative deviations from canceling; greater variance indicates more spread. If \(Z\) counts documents, variance is measured in squared document counts.

Since \(I_g^2=I_g\), \(\operatorname{Var}(I_g)=\mathbb E[I_g^2]-\mathbb E[I_g]^2=p(1-p)\). Multiplying by the fixed weight \(w_g\) also multiplies every deviation by \(w_g\), so squared deviations acquire a factor of \(w_g^2\): \(\operatorname{Var}(w_g I_g)=w_g^2\operatorname{Var}(I_g)\). Under group independence, these weighted variances add:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(N_{\mathrm{val}}) =p(1-p)\sum_g w_g^2. \]

The squared weights explain the influence of large groups. Suppose two groups contain 90 and 10 documents and \(p=0.2\). The expected validation count is 20, yet an individual split can contain only 0, 10, 90, or 100 documents. Exactly 20 is impossible. Replacing \(w_g\) with each group's token count under a fixed tokenizer gives the same derivation; long books can then dominate the variation. This is a model of independent random assignment, not a proof that a fixed SHA-256 output is random.

Report group counts, document counts, and length measures together. A production report should add token counts after the tokenizer is fixed. Our tokenizer has not yet been chosen, so this chapter's script reports UTF-8 bytes of document text. It does not label bytes as tokens or include JSON field names and serialization overhead in text length.

docs.title: Run a split with deliberate failure controls
docs.text:
The fixture examples/book/fixtures/split_records.jsonl contains 12 documents in ten groups. Two groups contain two documents each. One longer text reminds us that count and length are different measures. Run:

.venv/bin/python examples/book/split_walkthrough.py \
  --output outputs/book-split-v1 --seed 17

The script uses only the standard library and writes train.jsonl, validation.jsonl, test.jsonl, and split-report.json. It neither trains a model nor selects a seed using model scores. The report's groups field lists group buckets and assignments. totals records group and document counts, text UTF-8 bytes, and output file digests for each set. Document counts should sum to 12 and group counts to ten; inspect your report for the actual proportions.

The script also reverses traversal order and appends a new group before recomputing assignments. Successful checks produce:

{
  "order_independent": true,
  "existing_assignments_stable_after_append": true
}

Producing three files alone does not establish that a validator works. The script therefore constructs two deliberately incorrect alternatives in memory:

Failure control Deliberate change Expected rejection A group crosses sets Move one member of a multi-document group to another set group_leak Different groups share a complete text Keep group assignments but copy a text into another set normalized_content_leak

The first tests group boundaries; the second tests content boundaries. If the validator fails to reject either control, the script fails. These alternatives are never written into the normal split files. failure_probes records the intercepted reasons; an expected rejection message is not a failure of the valid split.

The content check applies NFC normalization and compares SHA-256 digests of complete texts. It detects the fixture's full-text duplication, but not a shared passage, changed names and numbers, or paraphrased questions. Digest collisions could also produce false alarms: a digest match is an interception signal, not a semantic judgment. The report's scope explicitly limits its claim to grouping and NFC full-text digest overlap.

Use a fresh output directory for another run to preserve prior evidence. A replacement --input must retain at least one multi-document group and populate at least two sets for the failure demonstrations to be meaningful. Otherwise the script rejects the demonstration instead of inventing a successful verification.

Additional metadata is retained with each document, so it too must remain valid JSON. This example rejects NaN, Infinity, and numbers outside the supported finite floating-point range, such as 1e999. Such a value at any nesting level stops the whole split before the output directory is created. The literal 1e999 is valid JSON number syntax; its rejection is a numeric-range limit of this reader, not a syntax error.

Field names must also be unique within each object. If a record contains two split_group fields, group identity is ambiguous before splitting begins; a parser must not silently choose one and then declare the groups separate. The reader rejects repeated names at every nesting level before writing outputs. This is an interoperability policy: the JSON standard describes differing implementation behavior when object names are not unique.

docs.title: Establish boundaries before encoding and packing
docs.text:
Documents should enter separate encoding pipelines after splitting. If we first concatenate every document into one token stream and then assign windows to training and validation, the windows can share substantial content: two windows of length 1,024 offset by one position overlap by 1,023 tokens. Those training instances are not independent evidence.

A clearer order is to establish related groups, split them, encode each set, and generate separate manifests. The current TokenDataset reads a continuous token stream described by one manifest; it does not create training, validation, and test boundaries automatically. Our script has produced real JSONL inputs for subsequent encoding. Do not recombine the three sets and sample windows from their joint stream.

A tokenizer is itself learned from data. For a strict unseen-data evaluation, restrict tokenizer training to the training set and encode validation and test with that frozen tokenizer. The next chapter distinguishes learning a tokenizer from using it to encode text.

docs.title: How to state a negative contamination result
docs.text:
Deduplication usually compares documents within training data. Evaluation contamination detection compares training inputs against evaluation objects. Some matching methods can be shared, but the comparison scope differs. A training corpus with no internal duplicates can still contain benchmark questions or answers.

Checks can start with full-text matches and extend to long substrings, normalized questions, or approximate similarity when appropriate. Each method has a coverage boundary: common short definitions can create false alarms, while paraphrases can evade detection. Record candidates, matching spans, comparison units, review outcomes, and methods that were not implemented.

After this chapter's script passes, a defensible conclusion is: “No group crosses sets, no cross-set NFC full-text digest overlap was detected within this check, and both failure controls were rejected.” It does not establish that the data is contamination-free, much less guarantee independence from every future evaluation. The tiny corpus cannot measure generalization quality either; it checks whether the split mechanism follows its rules.

Document membership is now fixed. Next we examine another choice that affects training: how the same text becomes an integer sequence, and how vocabulary and tokenization shape model inputs, outputs, and computation.

docs.title: 9 Tokenizer: from text to a fixed vocabulary
Why the same sentence can have different input lengths
docs.text:
When we read a sentence, we naturally recognize characters, words, and punctuation. A model receives integers. Before giving it “猫坐下” (“the cat sits down”), we must decide whether each Chinese character occupies one position or whether “坐下” is one unit. Does the English word cats occupy one position, or two positions for cat and s? A tokenizer makes these decisions before the neural network begins its computation.

Tokenization is broader than identifying complete words. A token can be a word, part of a word, a Chinese character, or a byte in a UTF-8 representation. Different tokenizers can produce different sequence lengths for the same text. A model that accepts 4096 tokens therefore does not necessarily accept 4096 Chinese characters or 4096 English words. Earlier chapters established which text belongs in the training distribution. We now decide how to represent that text as a discrete sequence.

For raw text \(u\), write the output of tokenizer \(\tau\) as

\[ \tau(u)=s=(s_1,\ldots,s_{n_u}),\qquad s_t\in\{0,\ldots,V-1\}. \]

Here \(n_u\) counts tokens produced from this text and \(V\) is the vocabulary size. Later, \(L\) retains its book-wide meaning as the number of model input positions in a window; one document can contribute several windows. A vocabulary maps tokens to integer IDs. Assigning 17 to “猫” and 42 to “坐下” is one possible teaching convention. The fact that 17 is smaller than 42 says nothing about their meanings: these integers are addresses for a lookup. Model training will learn the vectors stored at those addresses.

A tokenizer affects the number of training positions, context coverage, and parameter count. It is part of the training design. We will first work through a complete BPE example, then distinguish other common methods, and finally connect tokenization to the training script, model dimensions, and data shards.

docs.title: A vocabulary does not specify a complete tokenizer
docs.text:
Suppose a vocabulary contains c, a, t, ca, and cat. The string cat has at least three valid segmentations: c | a | t, ca | t, and cat. The vocabulary tells us which pieces are available, but not which segmentation to choose. The selection rules must also be saved.

A normalizer determines whether full-width letters become ordinary letters and whether certain Unicode representations are combined. A pre-tokenizer establishes initial boundaries within which further segmentation can occur. The encoder applies fixed segmentation rules and maps pieces to IDs. The decoder reconstructs text from IDs. Special tokens represent control information such as document boundaries and padding.

raw text → normalization → pre-tokenization → learned segmentation → vocabulary lookup → IDs
IDs → token lookup → decoding → recoverable text

The final result is “recoverable text” because an earlier operation may have discarded information. If normalization changes full-width Ａ to A, decoding cannot determine which form appeared originally. Saving a vocabulary while omitting the normalizer, merge order, or decoder does not save a complete tokenizer.

We must also distinguish two meanings of training. Tokenizer training learns a vocabulary and segmentation rules from text statistics. Language-model training learns embeddings, attention, MLPs, and other neural parameters from the encoded sequences. The small BPE experiment below needs neither a GPU nor a Transformer. Normally, we train and freeze the tokenizer before producing language-model training data.

docs.title: Training BPE from four word types
docs.text: BPE stands for byte-pair encoding. For text tokenization, it repeatedly replaces frequent adjacent symbol pairs with new symbols. The word “byte” reflects the algorithm's history; we will start with characters to keep the arithmetic visible and discuss bytes later. A primary reference for this application to subword segmentation is Sennrich et al.'s original paper.

docs.title: Decide what is being counted
docs.text:
The following corpus is constructed for this chapter. Each row represents a word type; its frequency is the number of occurrences in the full corpus. The four rows do not have equal weight.

Word type Frequency Initial symbol sequence cat 5 c · a · t · </w> cats 2 c · a · t · s · </w> cap 3 c · a · p · </w> caps 1 c · a · p · s · </w>

The dots only display boundaries between symbols; they are not corpus content. The end-of-word marker </w> is one indivisible symbol. It distinguishes “this word ends here” from “more characters follow.” It is a boundary symbol in this teaching algorithm, not the language model's EOS. We process words independently, never merge across words, and do not reconstruct sentence whitespace in this experiment.

There are six initial vocabulary symbols: c, a, t, p, s, and </w>. The corpus contains \(5+2+3+1=11\) word occurrences. Multiplying each word's symbol count by its frequency gives

\[ 5\times4+2\times5+3\times4+1\times5=47 \]

initial symbol positions. This includes eleven end markers, so it is not the raw character count. We need this counting unit before “reducing sequence length” becomes a precise statement.

Let \(f(w)\) be the frequency of word type \(w\), whose current symbols are \((q_1^{(w)},\ldots,q_{m_w}^{(w)})\). The weighted count of adjacent pair \((a,b)\) is

\[ C(a,b)= \sum_w f(w) \sum_{i=1}^{m_w-1} \mathbf{1}\!\left[q_i^{(w)}=a,\ q_{i+1}^{(w)}=b\right]. \]

The indicator \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\) equals 1 when its condition holds and 0 otherwise. The inner sum counts occurrences within one word type; the outer sum weights them by word frequency. Pair \((c,a)\) appears once in every word type, giving \(5+2+3+1=11\). Pair \((a,t)\) appears only in cat and cats, giving \(5+2=7\).

Here is the complete initial table, including low-frequency pairs:

Adjacent pair Contributing word types Weighted count (c, a) All four 11 (a, t) cat, cats 7 (t, </w>) cat 5 (a, p) cap, caps 4 (p, </w>) cap 3 (s, </w>) cats, caps 3 (t, s) cats 2 (p, s) caps 1

We are counting adjacent positions, not whether two characters occur anywhere in the same word. Pair (c,t) is not adjacent yet and is absent from the table.

docs.title: Recompute adjacency after every merge
docs.text:
The first round selects (c,a), the most frequent pair, and replaces it with ca. Each word type loses one position. Weighted by frequency, the corpus loses eleven positions, leaving \(47-11=36\).

cat   ×5: ca · t · </w>
cats  ×2: ca · t · s · </w>
cap   ×3: ca · p · </w>
caps  ×1: ca · p · s · </w>

Neither (c,a) nor (a,t) exists now. New adjacent pairs include (ca,t) and (ca,p). Selecting a second pair from the original table would try to merge symbols that are no longer there. Each round must update counts using the current sequences.

The table below lists every remaining candidate before each subsequent merge. The number after the colon is its weighted count; the first entry is the selected pair.

Round All current pairs and weighted counts 2 (ca,t):7; (t,</w>):5; (ca,p):4; (p,</w>):3; (s,</w>):3; (t,s):2; (p,s):1 3 (cat,</w>):5; (ca,p):4; (p,</w>):3; (s,</w>):3; (cat,s):2; (p,s):1 4 (ca,p):4; (p,</w>):3; (s,</w>):3; (cat,s):2; (p,s):1 5 (cap,</w>):3; (s,</w>):3; (cat,s):2; (cap,s):1

Round 2 merges ca · t into cat. Round 3 merges cat · </w> into cat</w>. That third merge changes the word type cat but leaves cats unchanged: in the latter, cat is followed by s. Round 4 merges ca · p into cap.

Round 5 has a tie: (cap,</w>) and (s,</w>) both have count 3. Our implementation first compares counts and then breaks ties by the ascending Unicode lexicographic order of the pair tuple. It compares the first strings, then the second strings if necessary. Since cap precedes s, it selects (cap,</w>). This is a rule of our teaching implementation, not a claim about every BPE library. Without an explicit tie rule, iteration order can affect the vocabulary.

The complete state after every round is shown below. Each transition replaces only the pair selected for that round.

State Added token cat × 5 cats × 2 cap × 3 caps × 1 Weighted positions Initial — c a t </w> c a t s </w> c a p </w> c a p s </w> 47 Round 1 ca ca t </w> ca t s </w> ca p </w> ca p s </w> 36 Round 2 cat cat </w> cat s </w> ca p </w> ca p s </w> 29 Round 3 cat</w> cat</w> cat s </w> ca p </w> ca p s </w> 24 Round 4 cap cat</w> cat s </w> cap </w> cap s </w> 20 Round 5 cap</w> cat</w> cat s </w> cap</w> cap s </w> 17

Five added symbols plus six initial symbols give eleven vocabulary entries. We retain the original characters even if some no longer appear individually in this corpus: new words may still require them.

No selected occurrences overlap in this example, so the reduction in positions equals the chosen pair's count at every round. This is not a universal identity. Sequence a a a has two adjacent occurrences of (a,a), but replacing non-overlapping occurrences from left to right gives aa a and removes only one position. The script implements that rule explicitly. Pair frequency and the number of actual replacements must not be treated as interchangeable in every corpus.

docs.title: Encoding applies merge ranks without learning new frequencies
docs.text:
Now consider catt, which was absent from training. Relearning a vocabulary from this input would make its representation depend on the current text and undermine the stable meaning of the IDs used to train the model. Ordinary BPE encoding applies the learned rules.

Assign each rule a merge rank in learning order. The script uses ranks starting at zero:

Rank Fixed rule 0 c + a → ca 1 ca + t → cat 2 cat + </w> → cat</w> 3 ca + p → cap 4 cap + </w> → cap</w>

Encoding starts from base symbols. Among current adjacent pairs that have a learned rule, it selects the smallest rank, applies the merge, and checks adjacency again. It stops when no rule applies.

c · a · t · t · </w>
    rank 0
ca · t · t · </w>
    rank 1
cat · t · </w>
    no applicable rule; stop

Even though cat</w> is in the vocabulary, it cannot be used here: another t follows cat. Another unseen word, catcap, uses ranks 0, 1, 3, and 4 to produce cat | cap</w>. Neither encoding adds a token or re-estimates corpus frequencies.

Token-to-ID lookup happens after segmentation. The teaching script sorts the initial symbols by Unicode order, then appends learned symbols in order. Thus catt becomes cat | t | </w> with teaching IDs [7, 5, 0]. These IDs belong only to this experiment and must not be copied into a model configuration. This example has no BOS, EOS, or PAD; ID 0 is the end-of-word marker.

Figure 9.1　Identify the four word types contributing to the count of eleven for (c,a), then trace the new word using frozen ranks. Merged ribbons retain their original spans: the second t prevents cat from being adjacent to the end marker, so rank 2 cannot apply. Vocabulary IDs are looked up only at the end; IDs and ranks serve different roles. Numbers are hand-derived from the corpus above.

Open SVG PNG · 2× Vector PDF TikZ Scroll on narrow screens; open the image for full size.

docs.title: Produce an artifact that can be checked against the arithmetic
docs.text:
The repository's examples/book/bpe_walkthrough.py uses only the Python standard library. Counting, merging, training, and encoding are separate functions. The two key decisions are visible directly:

# 训练：频次优先，同频时按 pair 字典序决定。
chosen = min(counts, key=lambda pair: (-counts[pair], pair))

# 编码：只在已有规则中选 rank 最小的一项。
pair = min(candidates, key=lambda candidate: ranks[candidate])

From the repository root in the prepared Linux experiment environment, run:

.venv/bin/python examples/book/bpe_walkthrough.py \
  --output outputs/book/bpe-walkthrough.json

The output contains the before-and-after sequences for every round, all pair counts, the final vocabulary, encoding traces for new words, the Python version, and the script's SHA-256. The theoretical calculation above predicts selected counts [11, 7, 5, 4, 3] and positions changing from 47 to [36, 29, 24, 20, 17]. Those are hand-computed expectations; the generated JSON is the evidence from your particular run.

The script refuses to overwrite an existing report; choose a new output filename for another run. It deliberately handles individual words over its known base alphabet and rejects “猫” because that character is absent. Being able to form unseen words does not imply being able to represent every writing system. Coverage needs a separate solution in a production tokenizer.

docs.title: WordPiece and Unigram make different segmentation decisions
docs.text: For each method, ask what training saves and how encoding selects a segmentation. Sharing the appearance of a subword vocabulary does not imply sharing an algorithm.

docs.title: One concrete meaning of WordPiece: BERT's encoder
docs.text:
Consider BERT's WordPiece encoder specifically. It starts at the left of a word and chooses the longest matching vocabulary piece. Pieces inside the word carry the prefix ##. If a teaching vocabulary contains cat and ##s but not cats, the word cats becomes cat | ##s. The prefix marks a continuation; it does not represent two literal hash characters.

If the remaining suffix cannot be segmented, BERT's implementation replaces that word with the unknown token rather than learning a new rule. This behavior can be checked in WordpieceTokenizer in BERT's original tokenization.py. We have specified that implementation's longest-match encoding. WordPiece vocabulary training should not be equated with the maximum-pair-count BPE procedure above, and this chapter does not implement a complete WordPiece trainer. The repository's production entry point supports BPE and Unigram.

docs.title: Unigram assigns probabilities to alternative segmentations
docs.text:
Unigram assigns a probability to each vocabulary piece. For candidate segmentation \(\sigma=(v_1,\ldots,v_K)\), the independent-piece assumption gives the score

\[ P(\sigma)=\prod_{j=1}^{K}p(v_j), \qquad \sum_{v\in\mathcal V}p(v)=1. \]

Here \(\mathcal V\) is the set of pieces. Independence is an assumption used by this segmentation model, not a claim that natural-language words are unrelated. These probabilities are also separate from the conditional probabilities learned by the later neural language model.

Use cat again with the following stipulated five-piece vocabulary:

Piece c a t ca cat \(p(v)\) 0.10 0.10 0.20 0.25 0.35

The probabilities sum to one. The three legal segmentations receive scores

\[ \begin{aligned} P([\texttt{cat}])&=0.35,\\ P([\texttt{ca},\texttt{t}])&=0.25\times0.20=0.05,\\ P([\texttt{c},\texttt{a},\texttt{t}])&=0.10\times0.10\times0.20=0.002. \end{aligned} \]

The maximum-score segmentation is cat. To sample among these segmentations, first normalize for the same observed string. The total score is \(0.402\), so the conditional probability of the single-piece segmentation is \(0.35/0.402\approx0.871\), not 0.35. Changing the piece probabilities can change the best segmentation. There are no merge ranks in this decision.

Long strings have too many segmentations to enumerate explicitly. Since logarithms are increasing, maximizing a product is equivalent to maximizing the sum of its logarithms. Let \(D(j)\) be the best log score for the first \(j\) characters, with \(D(0)=0\) for the empty prefix. Then

\[ D(j)= \max_{\substack{0\le i<j\\u_{i+1:j}\in\mathcal V}} \left[D(i)+\log p(u_{i+1:j})\right]. \]

The recurrence tries each possible starting point for the last piece and attaches it to the best preceding prefix. Recording the selected starting points lets us trace backward from the end and recover the segmentation. In the example, the best two-character score is \(\log0.25\). At the third character, comparing \(\log0.35\) with \(\log0.25+\log0.20\) selects the whole cat. Uncoverable prefixes receive a score of negative infinity.

The probabilities above were chosen for illustration. Training must estimate them and shrink the candidate vocabulary. If \(\mathcal S(u)\) contains every segmentation that concatenates to \(u\), training seeks to maximize the following log likelihood. A loss to minimize would require a minus sign in front of the entire expression:

\[ \mathcal J_{\mathrm{tok}} =\sum_u f(u)\log \left[ \sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal S(u)} \prod_{v\in\sigma}p(v) \right]. \]

First sum the scores of alternative segmentations of the same string, then accumulate log likelihood weighted by text frequency. Training alternates between estimating segmentation statistics and updating probabilities, while progressively removing less useful candidates and protecting required base characters. See Kudo's original Unigram subword-model paper. This section explains scores, best segmentation, and the training objective. It does not derive every EM update, candidate-generation step, or pruning operation; experiments use a pinned library implementation for those.

SentencePiece is a toolkit supporting methods including BPE and Unigram. Listing “BPE, Unigram, SentencePiece” as three algorithms at the same level mixes methods with their implementation tools.

docs.title: From character coverage to byte coverage
docs.text:
Character BPE can encode only characters in its initial alphabet. Enumerating every possible character is inconvenient for multilingual text. An alternative is to represent text as UTF-8 bytes. A byte has one of 256 values, from 0 to 255. If every base byte is representable, valid UTF-8 text can be decomposed into known units. Frequent byte sequences can then become BPE merges or pieces in a Unigram model.

Three operations must be distinguished. The ByteLevel pre-tokenizer maps bytes to character representations used by the segmentation algorithm. A complete initial alphabet requires the trainer to retain all 256 base representations, including those absent from the training sample. The ByteLevel decoder converts those representations back into bytes and text. Configuring the pre-tokenizer does not replace the other two steps. The BpeTrainer and UnigramTrainer APIs in Tokenizers 0.22.2 both accept initial_alphabet; the Unigram training source includes it among required characters.

The repository script now passes ByteLevel.alphabet() to both trainers and installs the decoder. Their segmentation algorithms remain different: BPE learns merge rules, while Unigram learns piece scores. A complete byte representation is also distinct from the <0xXX> unknown-character fallback protocol used by some other tokenizers.

With four additional special tokens, the requested vocabulary must contain at least \(256+4=260\) entries. This is a lower bound for fitting the base units, not a guarantee that training produces exactly the requested size. Small corpora, insufficient BPE pairs, or library training constraints can make the actual size differ. Model configuration must use the produced artifact.

docs.title: Complete bytes do not imply lossless recovery of the original text
docs.text:
The script applies NFKC normalization. Original text Ａ① 猫🙂 becomes A1 猫🙂. Recovering the latter demonstrates preservation of the normalized text; it does not recover the original full-width letter or circled digit. Compatibility distinctions preserved by NFC in the cleaning chapter can still disappear at this tokenizer stage, so the upstream cleaning rule alone does not establish an end-to-end lossless pipeline.

For ordinary text that is not interpreted as control tokens, with additional whitespace cleanup disabled, our check is therefore

\[ \operatorname{decode}\!\left(\operatorname{encode}(u)\right) =\operatorname{NFKC}(u), \]

not unconditional equality with \(u\). Disable automatic special-token insertion for this check, and include unseen Chinese characters, emoji, newlines, tabs, and compatibility characters. The --no-byte-level option uses Whitespace pre-tokenization instead. That experimental path does not preserve arbitrary original whitespace or guarantee complete byte coverage, so it cannot inherit this round-trip expectation. If an experiment must retain compatibility distinctions, choose a different normalization policy before training its tokenizer.

The repository also provides a training-free ByteTokenizer. Bytes 0–255 map to IDs 3–258; PAD, BOS, and EOS have IDs 0, 1, and 2. Its vocabulary size is 259, and it does not apply the NFKC normalization above. It is useful for checking data/model interfaces, but produces longer sequences: a common Chinese character typically occupies three UTF-8 bytes. Complete coverage and compact representation are separate properties.

docs.title: How vocabulary size fixes model input and output dimensions
docs.text:
An ID is not a vector. The model first uses an embedding matrix to look it up. For hidden width \(d\),

\[ E\in\mathbb R^{V\times d},\qquad s_t\longmapsto E_{s_t,:}\in\mathbb R^d. \]

Each token occupies a row, so a larger vocabulary means more rows. After several layers of computation, the model produces a hidden vector \(h\) of width \(d\). Predicting the next token requires a score for every vocabulary candidate:

\[ z=hW_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad W_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb R^{d\times V},\qquad z\in\mathbb R^V. \]

Here \(h\) is written as a row vector. The components of \(z\) are logits; softmax converts them to probabilities that sum to one. Once the vocabulary is fixed, the final classification head must output \(V\) scores. The MLP intermediate width can be chosen separately, but in this architecture its output returns to the residual width \(d\); the final vocabulary projection maps \(d\) to \(V\).

Input embeddings and the output projection may share parameters, called tied embeddings, by setting \(W_{\mathrm{out}}=E^{\mathsf T}\). Without tying, each matrix contains \(Vd\) parameters. With tying, only one copy is stored. Ignoring biases:

\(V\) \(d\) Parameters in one embedding, \(Vd\) 259 16 4,144 32,000 16 512,000 128,000 16 2,048,000 32,000 768 24,576,000 128,000 768 98,304,000

A larger vocabulary may encode common text in fewer positions, but requires larger embeddings and output projections. Rare tokens may also receive too few training examples. Vocabulary selection must consider compression, language and domain coverage, model size, and training budget together.

docs.title: Train and preserve a reusable tokenizer
docs.text:
The production entry point is scripts/train_tokenizer.py. The following assumes .tools/uv and .venv have already been prepared as described in the environment chapter. Add tokenizer dependencies while retaining other installed extras:

.tools/uv sync --frozen --inexact --python .venv/bin/python --extra tokenizer

Use only the training portion after cleaning, deduplication, and splitting. Do not include validation or test text when selecting the vocabulary. Even without training a neural network, seeing evaluation text can change the vocabulary and encoded lengths. Record the language and domain proportions of tokenizer training data as well: merges learned from a small English-only sample may be unsuitable for a bilingual model.

Prepare data/tokenizer/train.jsonl with one JSON object per line and a string field named text. This is a training-entry example; the repository does not supply that production corpus automatically:

.venv/bin/python scripts/train_tokenizer.py \
  --input data/tokenizer/train.jsonl \
  --output outputs/tokenizer-32k \
  --algorithm bpe --vocab-size 32000 --text-key text

The script writes JSONL text fields to temporary text files, converts CRLF/CR to LF, appends a newline after each record, and preserves embedded newlines. The tokenizer trainer therefore reads text-file lines; one temporary line need not correspond to one original JSONL document. Document-boundary protocols are handled later when preparing language-model data.

Byte-level processing is enabled by default. --algorithm unigram changes both model and trainer. --min-frequency affects only BPE; --max-piece-length affects only Unigram. The important coverage setting is:

initial_alphabet = sorted(pre_tokenizers.ByteLevel.alphabet())

# 两种 trainer 都传入同一套基础字节表示。
trainer = trainers.BpeTrainer(
    vocab_size=32_000,
    initial_alphabet=initial_alphabet,
    special_tokens=["<pad>", "<bos>", "<eos>", "<unk>"],
)

This fragment explains the configuration relationship; the script above remains the complete executable entry point. It also installs NFKC, the ByteLevel pre-tokenizer, and decoder, then saves a Hugging Face tokenizer directory. Its tokenizer_metadata.json records requested and actual vocabulary sizes, special IDs, normalizer, decoder, alphabet size, library versions, input digests, and the SHA-256 of tokenizer.json.

A digest identifies file contents. It does not guarantee that retraining under another library version, parallel schedule, or tie implementation reproduces identical bytes. The teaching BPE defines its tie rule explicitly; production experiments should preserve the pinned library environment and final artifact. The script rejects existing output directories and checks both source and actual training-text digests before and after training, refusing to save a tokenizer if either changes. Metadata records source and converted training-text digests separately. Use a fresh path and archive the complete directory with metadata for each experiment.

docs.title: Checks before connecting the tokenizer to data preparation
docs.text:
First check representation correctness: IDs are in \([0,V)\), special IDs do not conflict, unknown inputs have the intended behavior, and encode/decode agrees with the normalization policy. The repository's tests/test_tokenizer_training.py trains BPE and Unigram on ASCII-only text, then checks unseen Chinese characters, emoji, whitespace, and NFKC changes. This verifies coverage and interfaces, not language quality.

Second check encoding cost. For fixed raw text, let \(N_{\mathrm{bytes}}\) be its UTF-8 byte count and \(T\) its ordinary-token count. Report

\[ r_{\mathrm{tok/byte}}=\frac{T}{N_{\mathrm{bytes}}}. \]

Use the same raw text and byte-counting convention for both tokenizers, and state whether BOS/EOS are included. For the same 1000 bytes, 500 tokens give a ratio of 0.5 and 800 tokens give 0.8. The former uses fewer training positions; this does not establish better model quality.

Break the ratio down by language and domain, then inspect document-length distributions, truncation rates, UNK rates, and special-token frequencies. A global average can hide longer Chinese sequences, damaged code indentation, or frequent unknown tokens in a smaller language. Per-token cross-entropy is not directly comparable across tokenizers either: the events being predicted have changed.

Third check the special-token protocol. BOS marks a sequence start, EOS a sequence or document end, PAD padding, and UNK an unknown item. Their strings, IDs, insertion points, and loss treatment must agree. Declaring a BOS ID does not imply that every encode call inserts it automatically. Adding it again in data preparation can also create duplicates.

ttt.data provides ByteTokenizer and HuggingFaceTokenizer. The latter calls encode(add_special_tokens=False), then manually adds BOS according to configuration. Data preparation appends EOS. Current behavior is summarized below; the next chapter explains loss masks position by position.

Data path BOS EOS Loss mask Ordinary NPY Added by encode if a BOS ID exists Appended per document if an EOS ID exists No separate mask file; targets are valid by default Sharded ordinary LM Same Same BOS is 0; other tokens are 1 Sharded supervised data Added to prompt, not repeated for response Appended after response Prompt is 0; response and EOS are 1

Pass the fixed local tokenizer directory when producing shards. These are alternative experiments: replace corpus.jsonl with prepared data, and train the tokenizer before running the second command.

.venv/bin/python -m ttt.data --input corpus.jsonl \
  --output data/pretrain-byte --sharded --tokenizer byte

.venv/bin/python -m ttt.data --input corpus.jsonl \
  --output data/pretrain-bpe --sharded --tokenizer outputs/tokenizer-32k

The commands use separate output directories. The data manifest records the tokenizer name, vocabulary size, and input/shard digests. Archive special IDs, normalization, library versions, and tokenizer digests alongside the training script's metadata; do not assume the data manifest automatically includes them all. Loading a remote tokenizer also requires fixing its revision and local files. The current CLI does not expose a separate revision argument.

A tokenizer's identity includes its vocabulary, segmentation rules, and surrounding processing, not just vocabulary size. Replacing it requires rebuilding token shards and checking actual \(V\) against model configuration. Old IDs may remain in range while referring to different tokens. An existing checkpoint cannot be made compatible merely by changing vocab_size.

We now have a token stream with defined meaning. The next chapter turns that stream into fixed model windows: which positions become inputs, which become prediction targets, and how document boundaries affect supervision and visible context.

docs.title: 10. Packing, labels, and masks
The model does not receive a document
docs.text: The model receives integer arrays. We use teaching names input_ids, labels, and loss_mask for the mathematical objects \(X,Y,M\). The actual repository loader returns (tokens, masks); sequence_loss shifts tokens into inputs and targets. It does not receive a dictionary with those three teaching names.

docs.title: A four-token example
docs.text:
Use letters before using large integer IDs. Suppose a tokenizer produced [A, B, C, D]. A next-token example is

\[ X=(A,B,C), \qquad Y=(B,C,D). \]

The first row asks “after A, what comes next?”; the second asks “after A,B, what comes next?”; the third asks “after A,B,C, what comes next?”. With the book notation, for a token sequence \((s_1,s_2,s_3,s_4)\),

\[ X=(s_1,s_2,s_3),\qquad Y=(s_2,s_3,s_4). \]

The target at position \(i\) is therefore \(y_i=s_{i+1}\). If we accidentally set \(Y=X\), we train copying rather than next-token prediction. If we shift twice, the loss is still a number, but it describes a different prediction problem.

For a model sequence length of sequence_length, BatchStream requests sequence_length + 1 raw tokens. The argument length in TokenDataset.rows(starts, length) already means that raw count: it returns length tokens and length - 1 target weights. Thus rows(starts, 5) supplies four prediction positions, not five. BatchStream.next_batch_with_masks() passes those arrays to the training code. Inspect this shift before inspecting the model.

docs.title: What a mask means
docs.text:
A mask answers one narrow question: should this target contribute to the loss? It does not automatically answer whether the token is visible as context.

For example, a prompt can be visible to the model while its targets are masked out. In supervised training, the model sees the prompt, but we may only charge the loss for the response. Padding can also have mask value zero, because it is an alignment placeholder rather than a real target.

Consider the integer stream

\[ s=(10,11,12,2,20), \]

where 2 is EOS and the other IDs are invented for illustration. A length-four window has \(X=(10,11,12,2)\) and \(Y=(11,12,2,20)\). If 20 begins another document, a policy masking the boundary target could use

\[ M=(1,1,1,0), \]

so that the final cross-document target is ignored. A continuous-stream policy could use \(M=(1,1,1,1)\). The two policies estimate different conditional distributions. Adding EOS alone does not tell us which policy is in use; the input, labels, loss mask, and attention boundary must be documented together.

docs.title: From position losses to a weighted mean
docs.text:
If the model assigns probability \(p_i\) to the correct target, the position's cross-entropy is \(\ell_i=-\log p_i\). Giving the correct answer more probability reduces the penalty. Probabilities \(1/2\) and \(1/4\), for example, produce losses of approximately \(0.693\) and \(1.386\). We use natural logarithms, so the unit is the nat. Loss is not accuracy: confidence matters even when two predictions have the same correct/incorrect outcome.

Generated masks usually use \(m_i\in\{0,1\}\). The loader also accepts fractional values in \([0,1]\), interpreted as relative target weights. Define total weight \(W=\sum_{i=1}^{L}m_i\). The weighted mean is

\[ \mathcal L= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{L}m_i\ell_i}{W},&W>0,\\[6pt] 0,&W=0. \end{cases} \]

For losses \(2,4\) and weights \(1/4,1/2\), the weighted sum is \(2.5\), total weight is \(0.75\), and the mean is \(2.5/0.75=10/3\). Doubling both weights to \(1/2,1\) leaves the mean unchanged. Scaling all weights together should not change a mean; relative weights determine the result. With fractional weights, their sum is total supervision weight, not a literal token count.

The implementation selects a safe denominator of 1 only when \(W=0\). Using \(\max(W,1)\) would incorrectly replace \(0.75\) by 1 and return 2.5 in the example. An all-zero mask has no supervision and returns zero language-model NLL by convention. Data checks should still detect that window; zero does not indicate perfect prediction. This statement concerns NLL and does not automatically constrain auxiliary terms, such as those used by MoE models. Momentum or weight decay can update parameters even when the NLL gradient is zero, so an all-zero mask does not imply that the entire training step leaves parameters unchanged.

Across samples, reconstruct each weighted sum before dividing by the batch's total weight. A sample with 100 valid targets and mean loss 2, combined with two valid targets at mean loss 10, gives \((100\times2+2\times10)/102\approx2.157\), not \((2+10)/2=6\). Across devices, aggregate numerators and denominators under the same principle; a device with almost no supervision should not receive the same weight as one with many targets. tests/test_weighted_loss.py adds checks for fractional weights, outer gradients, zero weights, and sparse supervision across two devices; they have not been executed in this review.

The implementation replaces masked target IDs with a safe in-range ID before indexing logits, then selects zero for their loss. The safe ID prevents an indexing error; it is not a training target. This explanation assumes finite model logits: a mask does not repair numerical failures inside the model.

docs.title: Independent documents and continuous streams
docs.text:
There are two legitimate packing contracts:

  • Independent-document packing prevents attention and carried model state from reading earlier documents, and handles next-token targets at boundaries explicitly. A zero loss mask alone cannot provide this isolation: it removes a loss term but does not erase context. Such packing needs document-aware attention or separate calls with state reset.
  • Continuous-stream packing concatenates documents into one stream. It uses storage efficiently and may deliberately learn statistics around EOS, but it must state whether cross-document attention and loss are allowed.

The current prepare_data function writes one NPY file; prepare_sharded_data writes shards and a manifest. Both encode retained documents and append EOS when the tokenizer provides one. TokenDataset.rows selects a window by global offset, which can cross EOS and a physical shard boundary. Neither path creates a block attention mask that resets at EOS. Both retain continuous context rather than independent-document isolation.

Their supervision policies differ. A single NPY has no stored mask, so the loader assigns weight 1 to every target. The sharded path assigns zero weight to the opening BOS of each document. For two documents A and B, the byte tokenizer produces [1,68,2,1,69,2], where 1 is BOS and 2 is EOS. Reading the full stream yields target weights [1,1,1,1,1] from the single NPY and [1,1,0,1,1] from the shards. The third target is the second document's BOS predicted after the first document's EOS. Masking that target still allows predictions in B to read A. The sharded path also skips whitespace-only text, whereas the single-NPY path encodes it. Switching preparation entry points can therefore change supervision and the token stream; it must not be recorded merely as a storage-format change.

docs.title: Inspect a boundary with actual byte IDs
docs.text:
Run this example from the repository root on the target machine. It follows the ordinary sharded path's encoding rules for two one-character documents. Constructing each array explicitly makes the shift visible.

.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
from ttt.data import ByteTokenizer

tokenizer = ByteTokenizer()
tokens, stored_mask = [], []
for text in ("A", "B"):
    document = tokenizer.encode(text) + [tokenizer.eos_token_id]
    tokens.extend(document)
    stored_mask.extend([0] + [1] * (len(document) - 1))
print("tokens:", tokens)
print("X:", tokens[:-1])
print("Y:", tokens[1:])
print("M:", stored_mask[1:])
PY

ByteTokenizer maps bytes 65 and 66 to IDs 68 and 69, with BOS 1 and EOS 2. The expected stream is therefore [1,68,2,1,69,2]. After shifting:

Code index Input \(X\) Target \(Y\) \(M\) Meaning 0 1 68 1 Predict A after BOS 1 68 2 1 Predict EOS after A 2 2 1 0 Do not charge loss for the next BOS 3 1 69 1 Predict B after the second BOS 4 69 2 1 Predict EOS after B

The third row has no direct loss, but the fourth can still attend to the earlier A. Boundary supervision and access to earlier context are two separate properties; the loss mask controls only the first.

docs.title: Code path and a remote smoke command
docs.text:
The relevant path is:

  1. ttt.dataset.prepare_sharded_data writes token and mask shards plus manifest.json.
  2. TokenDataset verifies the manifest and maps global offsets to shards.
  3. BatchStream.next_batch_with_masks samples starts and returns (tokens, masks).
  4. ttt.inner_loop.sequence_loss shifts targets, applies the mask, and aggregates weighted NLL. The outer step combines samples using their supervision-weight sums, which equal valid-target counts only for binary masks.
  5. training.py uses the resulting loss for the outer update.

On a machine with the repository and Python environment already prepared, a small data conversion is:

.venv/bin/python -m ttt.data \
  --input examples/sample.jsonl \
  --output outputs/packing-sample \
  --tokenizer byte \
  --sharded \
  --shard-tokens 256

The command is a data-preparation example, not a claim that a local workstation has the required dependencies. The resulting manifest is the input to the next chapter. Record its digest before a long run.

docs.title: Checks and limits
docs.text:
Check that inputs, targets, and masks each have \(L\) positions, as in the short example. A stricter masked-target check fixes every input, mask, and initial state, changing only the final masked target ID; that ID should not affect the result through the loss term. Do not generalize this to arbitrary masked tokens, which may also be inputs for later predictions. A shape check alone cannot establish document isolation.

The next chapter turns token files, masks, hashes, and sampler state into a recoverable dataset object.

docs.title: Summary and next question
docs.text: Packing defines the window, label shift defines the prediction target, and the loss mask defines which targets receive supervision. EOS marks a boundary but does not by itself decide whether the following position is supervised. The next chapter stores these arrays with hashes and offsets in a recoverable dataset manifest.

docs.title: 11. Datasets, shards, and manifests
Why a directory is not a data version
docs.text:
Suppose a directory contains part-0.npy, part-1.npy, and a temporary file. A script that reads “all NPY files” has hidden assumptions about sorting, ignored files, vocabulary size, and masks. Copying the directory to another machine can silently change the token stream. A manifest makes those assumptions explicit and gives the loader something to verify.

In this book, a shard is a storage fragment, while a dataset is the logical ordered stream plus the rules that make it readable. A shard boundary is not automatically a document boundary.

docs.title: A minimal manifest
docs.text:
The current loader accepts a version-one manifest with the following essential shape:

{
  "format_version": 1,
  "vocab_size": 259,
  "shards": [
    {
      "tokens": "v-00000.npy",
      "mask": "v-00000.mask.npy",
      "count": 256,
      "sha256": "<token-file-sha256>",
      "mask_sha256": "<mask-file-sha256>"
    }
  ]
}

tokens and mask are filenames relative to the manifest directory. The loader rejects paths that escape that directory. This is a reproducibility and safety rule: an old manifest should not silently read a file from an unrelated absolute path on a new machine.

The vocabulary field matters even when every integer is in range. Suppose two vocabularies both contain 259 entries, but ID 68 means A in one and B in the other. Every stored ID can be legal and every file digest can match while the model receives different meanings. vocab_size checks vocabulary-size agreement, not the identity of equally sized mappings. The tokenizer version, special-token IDs, and tokenizer-file digest must also be recorded in the experiment record.

docs.title: What the loader verifies
docs.text:
TokenDataset.init performs several checks with different purposes:

  1. It checks format_version and vocab_size, so a new schema or model vocabulary cannot be mistaken for the old one.
  2. It recomputes SHA256 for every token and mask file. SHA256 is a digest, a short fingerprint of the bytes; a changed file should produce a different digest.
  3. It memory-maps non-empty, one-dimensional integer arrays. Memory mapping avoids loading every shard into the Python heap, but it does not remove storage latency.
  4. It checks that every token lies in \([0,V)\), where \(V\) is the vocabulary size. This prevents an embedding lookup from going out of range.
  5. It checks that each mask has the same shape as its token shard and values in \([0,1]\).
  6. It records cumulative end offsets, allowing a global position to be mapped to a physical shard.

A matching digest is evidence that bytes match the recorded version, assuming a trusted reference manifest and ignoring practically infeasible SHA256 collisions. It does not establish corpus quality, permission to use it, or immunity to later edits. Replacing both a shard and its recorded digest also defeats comparison with that replacement manifest. Source digests, tokenizer metadata, split records, and a trusted record of the intended version remain necessary.

docs.title: A worked cross-shard window
docs.text:
Use two tiny shards:

Physical shard Token contents Count Cumulative end v-00000.npy [10, 11, 12, 13] 4 4 v-00001.npy [20, 21, 22, 23, 24] 5 9

These ends use half-open code-index intervals: shard 0 covers global positions [0,4), and shard 1 covers [4,9). For start=2 and length=5, the requested global positions are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. searchsorted([4,9], 2, side='right') selects shard 0, so the loader reads local offsets 2 and 3 ([12,13]), then continues at local offsets 0, 1, and 2 in shard 1 ([20,21,22]):

global positions: 2, 3 | 4, 5, 6
physical shard:   v-0   | v-1
local offsets:       2, 3 | 0, 1, 2
tokens:            12,13 | 20,21,22

The endpoint shows why side='right' matters. Global position 4 belongs to the second shard at local offset \(4-4=0\). searchsorted([4,9], 4, side='right') returns shard index 1; the default left search would return 0 and assign the position to the already ended first shard.

In this example, length=5 is the raw count and supplies four prediction positions. If the model's configured input length is 5 instead, the training path reads six raw tokens before shifting labels. A shard boundary does not insert EOS and does not reset attention; it is only a storage boundary. Document isolation comes from tokenization and packing policy, not from the fact that two arrays have different filenames.

docs.title: Three identities to keep
docs.text:
There are three useful layers of identity:

  • A shard digest detects replacement or corruption of one physical file.
  • A manifest digest detects changed shard order, counts, vocabulary, or metadata.
  • A source digest connects derived tokens back to the input records used to create them.

If someone reorders two shards, every shard digest still matches but the training sequence changes. Comparison with a trusted manifest digest catches that. Replacing a shard while retaining its trusted manifest triggers a digest mismatch. The loader checks the bytes available during loading; it does not lock files against later modification. Published data directories should be treated as immutable versions. Neither digest explains which original JSONL file was used, so the source digest remains part of provenance.

prepare_sharded_data assigns a random UUID version and rejects an existing manifest at the start. Use a single writer per output directory: that existence check is not a multiprocess write lock. Two identical runs do not receive the same version. Content-addressed versioning would instead derive identity from input and complete processing configuration, including the format version.

docs.title: The source digest must describe consumed bytes
docs.text:
Hashing the source only after processing leaves a provenance gap. Suppose the preparer has read {"text":"A"} and written A's tokens. Another process then replaces the source with {"text":"Z"}. A final-only source hash attaches Z's identity to A's tokens. The shards are intact, so ordinary shard verification cannot detect this mistake.

The preparer now hashes the source before reading, hashes the raw bytes actually consumed while reading, and hashes the source again before publishing the manifest. All three must agree. Blank lines and CRLF line endings participate in the consumed digest because source identity describes complete bytes, not just parsed JSON values. A mismatch prevents manifest publication. Some shard files may already have been written when preparation fails; without a successful manifest referencing them, they are not a completed dataset version.

This binds the output to consumed bytes and detects differences between the compared versions. It does not prove that the source never changed during processing: a file could change and be restored, or change after the final check. Formal preparation should still use immutable, read-only input versions. Regressions in tests/test_dataset.py change A to Z during encoding and require failure without a manifest, and separately cover blank lines and CRLF in the source digest. They were written but not executed in this review.

docs.title: Global offsets and windows
docs.text:
Let shard lengths be \((n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_K)\) and define cumulative ends

\[ e_0=0,\qquad e_j=\sum_{k=1}^{j} n_k. \]

A zero-based global position \(p\) belongs to shard \(j\) satisfying \(e_{j-1}\le p<e_j\), at local offset \(p-e_{j-1}\). searchsorted returns the zero-based shard index \(j-1\). For example, \(p=6\) in the second shard gives local offset \(6-4=2\), containing token 22. A window can read the end of one shard and the beginning of the next without changing logical order. Changing physical shard size should preserve every valid window provided both tokens and masks remain identical. The preceding chapter explains why switching between the single-NPY and sharded preparation entry points does not automatically meet that condition: their mask and empty-text policies differ.

The same distinction matters for document boundaries: physical storage is not semantic structure. If document offsets are needed for contamination checks or interpretability, add a document-offset sidecar linked to source record IDs. The current manifest does not provide complete token-to-document reverse lookup; shard filenames and token offsets alone cannot recover that provenance.

docs.title: Dataset state and sampler state
docs.text:
The dataset answers “what tokens exist?” The sampler answers “which window comes next?”. BatchStream uses a NumPy generator to sample starts and stores generator state, data SHA256, sequence length, batch size, and seed in state_dict().

Restoring only the seed is insufficient. A pseudo-random generator has an internal state that advances after every draw. Restoring the same seed restarts the sequence instead of continuing it. Restoring the generator state without checking the data fingerprint is also unsafe: the same random state can select different tokens from a changed dataset.

sample_rows(step, indices) derives independent windows from a SeedSequence built from the seed, step, and index. This is useful for fixed probes and evaluation, but it is a different sampling protocol from next_batch_with_masks. Reports should name which protocol produced a metric.

docs.title: Remote inspection example
docs.text:
Run this single snippet from the repository root on the prepared remote CPU node. It uses the repository JSONL fixture. If outputs/dataset-sample/manifest.json is absent, it generates shards with at most 256 tokens each. If it exists, the snippet checks the input digest and byte-encoding mode before reading it, without overwriting the manifest. Use a new output directory for another data version; do not edit the old manifest to bypass a mismatch. This command was not executed during the manuscript review.

We read two raw windows of five tokens. The first starts two positions before the first shard ends and crosses into the second; the second begins exactly at that boundary. Each produces four inputs, four targets, and four target-mask values. The rows method has already removed the first mask column, so the returned mask must not be shifted again.

.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from ttt.data import ByteTokenizer
from ttt.dataset import TokenDataset, file_sha256, prepare_sharded_data

source = Path("examples/sample.jsonl")
output = Path("outputs/dataset-sample")
manifest_path = output / "manifest.json"
if not manifest_path.exists():
    prepare_sharded_data(source, output, ByteTokenizer(), shard_tokens=256)

manifest = json.loads(manifest_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
if (manifest["input_sha256"] != file_sha256(source)
        or manifest["tokenizer"] != "byte"
        or manifest["supervised"] is not False):
    raise ValueError("Existing data differs from this recipe; use a new output directory.")

dataset = TokenDataset(manifest_path, ByteTokenizer.vocab_size)
if len(dataset.shards) < 2 or dataset.shards[0].size < 2 or dataset.shards[1].size < 5:
    raise ValueError("This example needs two shards with at least 2 and 5 tokens.")
boundary = int(dataset.ends[0])
starts = [boundary - 2, boundary]
tokens, masks = dataset.rows(starts, 5)
expected = np.stack([
    np.concatenate([dataset.shards[0][-2:], dataset.shards[1][:3]]),
    dataset.shards[1][:5],
])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(tokens, expected)
if tokens.shape != (2, 5) or masks.shape != (2, 4):
    raise ValueError("Unexpected window or target-mask shape.")

report = {
    "scope": "two_windows_at_first_shard_boundary",
    "manifest_sha256": dataset.fingerprint,
    "cumulative_ends": dataset.ends.tolist(),
    "starts": starts,
    "tokens": tokens.tolist(),
    "X": tokens[:, :-1].tolist(),
    "Y": tokens[:, 1:].tolist(),
    "M": masks.tolist(),
    "matches_direct_shard_read": True,
}
path = output / "rows-check.json"
path.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))
PY

Initial generation produces the manifest, token/mask shards, and their digests. A successful inspection also writes outputs/dataset-sample/rows-check.json, containing actual cumulative ends, starts, raw tokens, \(X,Y,M\), and the manifest digest. The tokens shape should be [2,5]; the three derived arrays have shape [2,4]. Comparing against direct reads of the two shard arrays checks token order for these two windows. Printing their masks helps inspection; it does not validate every window or document-boundary semantics.

The manifest stores each shard's count, not start or end. The report's cumulative_ends is computed by the loader. On disagreement, inspect shard order, counts, array lengths, side='right', and local offsets. A digest or vocabulary failure requires recovering the intended data version, not merely replacing recorded digests. A later successful inspection updates the report; an exception writes no new report, so an old file does not establish success for the current attempt.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Memory mapping reduces host memory pressure but random windows can still be storage-bound. Very small shards increase file and hash overhead; very large shards are harder to copy and recover. The teaching implementation prioritizes explicit validation and resumability. Distributed prefetch, cache policy, and source-aware sampling are later engineering layers.

The next chapter separates file layout from the statistical mixture of data sources.

docs.title: Summary and next question
docs.text: A dataset provides a verifiable logical token stream; a shard is a storage fragment; the manifest records shard order and identity. The sampler separately chooses the next window. Recovery needs the data digest, generator state, and window protocol in addition to a seed. The next chapter asks which sources produced those windows and how a sampler realizes a target recipe.

docs.title: 12. Data mixtures: deciding what the model reads
Storage size cannot choose the recipe
docs.text:
Once web text, code, and books are ready, one question remains: how much of the next billion training tokens should come from each source? Putting all files in one directory does not answer it.

Suppose web text occupies 900 GB and code and books occupy 50 GB each. Web text accounts for 90% of bytes, not necessarily 90% of tokens. Languages, formats, and tokenizers can have different token counts per byte. We must tokenize consistently before discussing training shares. For a concrete teaching example, instead assume the sources contain 800, 150, and 50 million usable tokens. Their concatenated token shares are then \(0.8,0.15,0.05\).

A large source is not necessarily more useful; it may simply be easier to obtain. Equalizing sources is not automatically better either, since a small collection may be read repeatedly. A recipe must address both coverage and repeated use.

docs.title: Specify the sampling unit
docs.text:
“Code is 20%” could mean 20% of documents, windows, or valid training positions. These coincide only under additional assumptions.

Suppose we select a source and then sample one window from it. If every window contains exactly \(L\) valid targets, source-selection probability \(p_j\) also determines the long-run valid-token share. If source \(j\) contributes an average of \(k_j\) valid targets per window, its valid-token share is instead

\[ q_j=\frac{p_j k_j}{\sum_i p_i k_i}. \]

This follows from counting: over \(n\) selections, source \(j\) is selected \(np_j\) times in expectation and contributes approximately \(np_jk_j\) valid positions. Dividing by the total cancels \(n\).

For example, two sources may each receive half the windows, while contributing 100 and 25 valid positions per window. Their valid-token shares become \(50/(50+12.5)=80\%\) and \(20\%\). The sampler has not failed; the mistake is equating half the windows with half the valid tokens. Both recipe and consumption report must specify their unit.

docs.title: Control source proportions with an exponent
docs.text:
Normalize the available token counts:

\[ w_j=\frac{N_j}{\sum_i N_i}, \]

where \(N_j\) is source \(j\)'s usable token count. One explicit way to reduce the dominance of large sources is

\[ p_j(\alpha)=\frac{w_j^\alpha}{\sum_i w_i^\alpha}, \qquad \alpha>0. \]

We call \(\alpha\) the mixture exponent rather than relying on an ambiguous temperature convention. At \(\alpha=1\), proportions remain unchanged. Values between zero and one compress disparities, while values above one amplify them. For two positive weights,

\[ \frac{p_i}{p_j}=\left(\frac{w_i}{w_j}\right)^\alpha. \]

If \(w_i>w_j\) and \(0<\alpha<1\), the new ratio is smaller than the original ratio, although the larger source remains larger. As \(\alpha\) approaches zero from above, positive-weight sources approach equal probability. An empty source still cannot be sampled.

For \(w=(0.8,0.15,0.05)\) and \(\alpha=0.5\),

\[ w^\alpha\approx(0.8944,0.3873,0.2236),\qquad p\approx(0.5942,0.2573,0.1485). \]

Books rise from 5% to about 14.85%. The cost is also visible: a billion-token budget would consume about 148.5 million book tokens from a collection containing only 50 million, or 2.97 times its available volume. This estimates average coverage; overlapping random windows do not read every position exactly three times.

Some systems use \(w_j^{1/T}\) instead. Their temperature \(T\) is the reciprocal of our exponent, so \(T<1\) has the opposite effect. Reproduction requires the formula and parameter, not just “temperature 0.5.”

docs.title: Budget and source exhaustion
docs.text:
With total valid-token budget \(N_{\mathrm{budget}}\), the ideal allocation is \(q_jN_{\mathrm{budget}}\). If this exceeds the available data, decide in advance whether to stop training, sample with replacement, or renormalize among surviving sources.

These choices define different experiments. Stopping changes the total budget, replacement changes repetition, and renormalization changes the later distribution. Silently switching sources after exhaustion makes the original recipe an inaccurate description of the run.

Logs should distinguish selected windows, input tokens, and summed valid mask weights. With binary masks the last quantity counts valid positions; fractional masks instead require the term weight sum. Source identity must also survive packing: a window crossing sources cannot be assigned wholly to the source of its first token.

docs.title: A recipe calculation to inspect and save
docs.text:
The current trainer samples from one logical token stream and does not consume a source-mixture recipe. The following standalone calculation runs on the target Linux machine after environment setup. It saves the example above without changing training behavior.

.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
import json
from pathlib import Path

counts = {"web": 800_000_000, "code": 150_000_000, "books": 50_000_000}
alpha = 0.5
total = sum(counts.values())
weights = {name: (count / total) ** alpha for name, count in counts.items()}
normalizer = sum(weights.values())
recipe = {
    "kind": "teaching_plan_not_connected_to_trainer",
    "formula": "p_j = (N_j / sum(N)) ** alpha / sum_i((N_i / sum(N)) ** alpha)",
    "alpha": alpha,
    "selection_unit": "equal_valid_length_window",
    "target_tokens": 1_000_000_000,
    "exhaustion_policy": "with_replacement",
    "sources": [
        {"name": name, "available_tokens": counts[name], "probability": value / normalizer}
        for name, value in weights.items()
    ],
}
path = Path("outputs/mixture-example/recipe.json")
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
path.write_text(json.dumps(recipe, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
for source in recipe["sources"]:
    print(source["name"], f'{source["probability"]:.4f}')
PY

The formula predicts printed probabilities of approximately 0.5942, 0.2573, and 0.1485, in that order. The JSON lets us inspect the calculation and budget. It does not establish that training used the recipe: that requires a sampler consuming the definition and logs recording actual consumption.

docs.title: Why short-run proportions fluctuate
docs.text:
A source probability of \(p=0.2\) does not force exactly one selection in every five. Assume \(n\) independent selections with unchanged probability. Let \(I_k\) be 1 when selection \(k\) chooses the source and 0 otherwise. The observed proportion is

\[ \hat p=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n} I_k. \]

Since \(\mathbb{E}[I_k]=p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(I_k)=p(1-p)\), independence lets us add variances:

\[ \mathbb{E}[\hat p]=p,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat p)=\frac{p(1-p)}{n}. \]

At \(n=100\), the standard deviation is 0.04, or four percentage points. Observing 17% once does not establish a sampler bug. This calculation counts independent source selections; 1,000 correlated tokens within one window are not 1,000 independent selections.

docs.title: Restoring the same distributed plan
docs.text:
Processes on multiple GPUs need assigned sample identities. One design derives the source and window from a global sample index, then distributes disjoint indices across processes:

\[ (\text{source},\text{window start}) =f(\text{seed},\text{recipe version},\text{data version},\text{sample index}). \]

This describes a proposed source-level design. The current code already has stateless sampling for single-stream windows, but lacks the complete source selection, exhaustion handling, and consumption log. Restoring only the integer step is insufficient: the function and its version, data fingerprint, global batch, and index assignment must also agree.

Compare the source and start-index sequence of an uninterrupted run with an interrupted-and-resumed run. Sample indices must not be skipped or duplicated. Sampling with replacement may legitimately assign the same window to different indices; that is a revisit, not a restoration error. The next chapter brings these recipe, data, and model conditions together before training.

docs.title: 13. Preflight: inspect inputs before starting a long run
An openable file is not enough
docs.text:
Suppose training immediately fails with an out-of-vocabulary target. The GPU, compiler, and model have already started, but the cause may be simple: the data uses a 32K tokenizer while the model has only 259 output positions. We do not need thousands of training steps to discover this. Checking data, tokenizer, model, and run configuration together is preflight.

Preflight looks for contradictions among inputs. It differs from evaluation: intact files and valid labels do not establish representative data, and a finite tiny-model loss does not establish language ability. First ask whether the declared experiment can execute, then whether its results are useful.

docs.title: Follow one target through the checks
docs.text:
A target ID must belong to the intended tokenizer vocabulary. Even an in-range integer can mean different text under another tokenizer. Checking \(0\le y<V\) is therefore insufficient; tokenizer files, normalization rules, and special-token semantics also need fixed identities.

The model must then be able to assign probability to that target. The current sharded loader requires the manifest vocabulary size to equal the model vocabulary size passed to it. This is a repository interface constraint, not a theorem about every language model: a larger output vocabulary can be mathematically valid, but does not bypass this version check. Editing the manifest number also cannot make data from another tokenizer compatible.

Third, the target must come from the right position. A length-\(L\) next-token prediction requires \(L+1\) consecutive tokens.
